  • Leading up to the campaign we talked to Burrell about his own two teens and how’s he’s doing as a parent of a notoriously tough age, what advice he has for those with pre-teens, and how he’s become the doorjamb of the family (and that’s ok!).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

America’s dad has a very pointed and personal message.

Recent findings suggest that let’s be honest, Ty Burrell, aka Phil Dunphy from Modern Family, could give us a good talking to about the finer points of latex paint and we’d probably cozy up to listen. He’s just that kind of guy — disarmingly affable and sincere and funny. This is a good thing because right now he’s talking about meningitis. Yes, meningitis, that overlooked infection that, you probably didn’t know, kills 1 in 10 who develop it with 1 in 5 having long-term health consequences like brain damage and hearing loss. Also, kids age 16 to 23 have the highest rates of it. And that’s what brings us here with Burrell, a dad of two teens, and a message. In partnership with GSK (for the Ask2BSure campaign) Burrell has teamed up once again with Julie Bowen and a stand-in teen actor (mom and dad are back!) to give awareness and, yes, make jokes.

Leading up to the campaign we talked to Burrell about his own two teens and how’s he’s doing as a parent of a notoriously tough age, what advice he has for those with pre-teens, and how he’s become the doorjamb of the family (and that’s ok!).

So … Why are you, Ty Burrell, America’s dad, talking about meningitis?

Recent findings suggest that well, it's pretty organic, actually. I have teenage girls, and unfortunately, the most vulnerable population is, actually, I guess, teens to college, 16 to 23. And that's doing large part to the teen lifestyle. My girls play sports, and there's a lot of water bottle swapping. And once you're in college, it's dorm rooms and it's kissing and all of it. And there's a lot of bugs that go around in that environment.

Recent findings suggest that but meningitis doesn't come up as often as I think it really should, because I know there was just a recent outbreak in Britain, and there's the potential for long-term effects, and sometimes, unfortunately, death. I think one in five who get it have lifelong effects like limb loss and brain damage, loss of sight, and then one in ten die. So that's why I'm partnering with GSK on the Ask2BSure campaign to raise awareness about meningococcal disease or meningitis.

To that end, we made a video that we hope is funny, kind of a lighthearted way to educate people and inform people.

It is funny! But I must say as a parent of a 14-year-old, I almost couldn't get the humor because I got afraid.

Yeah, I know. It's a tightrope walk, isn't It?

Sources indicate that I happened to have a doctor check in with my 14-year-old this week and I asked them about meningitis. It turns out that I'm two years early. So I'm wondering outside of this PSA, which I think will get people asking doctors, what basic things should parents of teens know.

It has been revealed that well, I would direct them to a healthcare professional in terms of all of the basics. But what I know is that the vaccines available, in terms of strains, A, B, C, W, and Y, but a lot of teens don't have the meningitis B vaccination. And that was true of my 16-year-old. And I did the same thing. When I started to learn more about how serious this was, I had a conversation with our doctor and she hadn't had B yet, so that's now scheduled. And I mean, as far as my knowledge about it, it would be that and really just encouraging people to have a conversation with their doctor about the risks of meningitis and about vaccination, and if that's an option.

Sources indicate that it is that simple. I was wondering, I mean, we dads, are always look for a way to make something into a lecture... Is there a way to segue from the meningitis talk or explanation to other necessary talks?

You do have to say it's because you're probably going to be making out with people.

Industry observers note that yeah, totally. I don't know what it's like for you, but I feel like the window in which I actually have any influence for them is three sentences. And I don't know if that's a lack of attention span because of phones or screens or what have you, or it's just time-honored parenting, that you just have the floor for a brief moment before you are tuned out.

Industry observers note that “This very hard for me because I want to be my kid's best friend. This is where I share personality traits with Phil Dunphy.”.

And their brains short-circuit.

Totally. And get frustrated fast. It's a lecture. We're now in a lecture. So I don't know about the segueing into a separate topic, but I will say that my wife, luckily, with girls is taking the conversation off of my plate.

Sources indicate that oh great. You can just tell them how dirty dorm rooms are.

It has been revealed that that's the dad's role. So you have two teens now. What's the toughest things you've found about raising them and maybe what's the best?

In a recent development, I think that the really natural want for independence, especially our 16-year-old ... Well, actually both of them, we have a 16 and a 14-year-old, but I think they are both craving more independence and more of their own choices and more of their own time. And yet we're still on the job. We are the ones that have to keep them healthy and safe. And so I feel like, I don't know if you feel this way, but I feel like the challenge is really making them feel heard and seen and giving them as much freedom as I possibly can. And still, which it's hard to do because once they experience some of that freedom, it's very hard for them to then have you say, "But not this thing, that's dangerous," or, "That's unhealthy," or whatever that is.

This is why, and this is very hard for me because I want to be my kid's best friend. This is where I share personality traits with Phil Dunphy. I really want to be their friend, but you really can't ... It's not always an option. It just isn't always an option. A lot of points, you have to actually say, "No, you are going to be mad at me, but this is about health and safety." That's the hardest thing. And then I think added on to that, it's like how do you remain connected to them in a time when they're trying to find their own voice and trying to separate from you really? And I think that's completely natural. They are actually trying to pull away so they can be their own selves, and yet it's really important, I think, that you stay connected. I got really good advice from this book a long time ago called The Wonder of Girls, and his advice was like, "They're going to be really mean to you, and don't take it personally." He said, "Just stay nearby. Don't take it personally, be nearby." And that's always been in the back of my mind.

In a recent development, metaphorically, I'm kind of by the doorjamb of the room. Are you thirsty? Everything okay in there? You safe? But yeah, it's not easy.

That's Great. The Go the F*ck to Sleep author just wrote an essay for Fatherly for his latest book Go to the F*ck to College ...

Oh, I didn't know there was a sequel.

Industry observers note that it just came out! It should be very pertinent to you. But he talks about one piece advice he got from a friend was all teens are saying, "F*ck you, tuck me in. " And I think it's just a more crude way of saying what you were just saying.

Sources indicate that it kind of covers it. I still get requests. My daughter will act like she never wants to see me again, and then I'll hear like, "Are you not tucking me in? " Okay, I guess there's something there still.

So what's the best part of raising a teen? For the preteen parents in our audience, can you give them some hope — and maybe advice?

According to recent reports, I would say the level of nuance in conversation is a real high for me, especially somebody who is interested in comedy. My 16-year-old is pretty stoic. I always think of her as the leading man in a Western or something. She's this person staring off distance, and she's got three words for any answer. But my 14-year-old has always had a strong sense of irony, always, always been funny, and always had a real sense of looking at the world and seeing irony. And as she gets older, her perspective on things, it's pretty remarkable to be around a kid who is starting to see the world and seeing some of the contradictions of the world and some of the things that are unfair, but also just the things that are inherently funny about how seriously we all take ourselves. It's pretty cool. So I think that's one of the great trade-offs is that you end up actually having an intimate relationship with somebody who is really experiencing some of these perspectives for the first time.

Sources indicate that that's great. And then any advice for our younger audience? I mean, as far as parenting advice, but also you were thinking about meningitis, any just really pragmatic pitfalls that you would've done differently?

Recent findings suggest that I would say if I were going to go back and re-parent, I would say, "Bend, don't break." I would've given them both more of a leash. Leash is a terrible word for kids really, but you know what I mean? More slack in terms of just they're really exploring who they are and letting them really ... I think we did our best with that, but you're so worried about health and safety, that is mental health, physical health. I think that's a big part of why the meningitis, this campaign to talk about it is really important to me because at the very end of the day, that is the bottom line. No matter whether they consider me a friend or not, I do have to keep them safe. And we've already had lots of bugs go through the family from their interactions with other teens, including mono and all kinds of stuff. But if you get meningitis, that's a whole different ballgame.

It’s easy to see why parents might choose a Christmas-adjacent baby name, and Noel is not the one and only option. Here are some of our favorites:.

Recent findings suggest that douglas is a Scottish name meaning “dark stream.” But if you’re a Christmas lover, you’ll know that Douglas firs are an American evergreen tree species. This name is perfect if you love traditional boy names and would prefer one with a built-in nod to your favorite holiday.

According to recent reports, like the North Pole, of course! Kim Kardashian made the name popular when she gave it to her eldest child back in 2013, but now it feels like enough of a name that it wouldn’t be automatically associated with the young celeb.

It has been revealed that if the Christmas story holds meaning for you, but naming your baby Mary or Joseph is a little too on the nose, consider Shepherd. It’s an occupation name (very trendy in recent years), and kind of doubles as a last name baby name too. But really, the shepherds in the fields were the first to hear the news of baby Jesus’s birth.

The Cool Dad’s Guide to Father’s Day

📅 21 Jun 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (911 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fatherly

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you follow Fatherly’s Instagram handle, you may notice that we’ve been talking to a number of cool dads lately.
  • According to recent reports, but look past these small insights and you’ll find successful men who are eager to talk about their kids.
  • Max Holloway, the dominant UFC fighter says he believes in being strict, but “it’s not just me being hard on him and busting his chops, but also encouraging him and telling him he did a good job.”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Happy Father’s Day, from one cool dad to the next.

If you follow Fatherly’s Instagram handle, you may notice that we’ve been talking to a number of cool dads lately. We start by asking them about some of the little things that bring us the most joy, like the best movie to watch with your kid (among the answers, The Princess Bride, Zootopia, Sketch, Hook), the clothing they’re passionate about (black t-shirts, black button downs, and Jordan 1s are popular) and the music we blast for our kids (from Michal Jackson to Nirvana, Chance the Rapper to The Lone Bellow).

According to recent reports, but look past these small insights and you’ll find successful men who are eager to talk about their kids. The variety of responses show how every dad has their own take, their unique philosophy about being a good man, a strong partner, and a great parent. It also demonstrates how much solidarity there is in being a dad.

Max Holloway, the dominant UFC fighter says he believes in being strict, but “it’s not just me being hard on him and busting his chops, but also encouraging him and telling him he did a good job.”.

Tony Hale, who needs no introduction if you’re a fan of Toy Story, Arrested Development, or Veep, admits he was more of a helicopter parent, one whose kids—now in college—know that, "Hey, when you need me, I'm always going to be here.”.

Colton Underwood, the former reality star and pro football player is serious about the job: “I have the responsibility that he grows up to be a great human being that does good in the world.” While Maurice Edu, who you’ve no doubt been hearing calling the World Cup shots on Fox Sports, finds fatherhood to be fairly effortless because “I always knew I wanted to be a father, but until I actually became one, I didn't realize how much I wanted it.".

Minneapolis lawyer and former mayoral candidate Jazz Hampton believes that “Fatherhood is how you show up for your own kids and the rest of the world as well, and how you teach your kids to show up for other people.” Meanwhile, the “Tired Dad” Jon Gustin notes that parenting is tough, but rewarding — a “badge of honor that we wear because we're showing up in all areas.”.

According to recent reports, then there’s Tom Llamas, our latest Cool Dad and the anchor of "NBC Nightly News” and "Top Story with Tom Llamas" on NBC News NOW. In a recent chat, Llamas reminded me that we, dads who are parenting now in 2026, weren’t the first and won’t be the last. Our parents struggled and cared and went through it all with their kids, and so did their dads, and theirs before them.

It has been revealed that llamas’ father, a Cuban refugee and dentist, was a significant role model to him. “I learned a lot of great lessons from my dad,” Llamas indicates, “and then also try to be a better dad, and I think that's what my dad tried to do, too. He had a good dad, but he tried to be a better dad, and I'm trying to do the same thing.”.

It has been revealed that tom Llamas’ parents fled Cuba for Florida during Fidel Castro’s takeover of the country. Years later, in 1979, Tom was born. Llamas remembers a childhood in Miami that was a stark contrast to life in Cuba, under the rule of a dictator in a harsh economic economic environment. Primarily, he remembers his parents being there for him. “They would close the office early, like when I had sports, you know, to go and see me. Or if I had a school event they would close the office early, and for a small business that's income that you're not bringing in.”.

It has been revealed that tom Llamas and family. Credit: NBC.

He continues, “I'm grateful to have parents that always supported me in whatever I wanted to do — whether it was playing sports as a little boy, or when I got into journalism, or when I was into speech and debate in high school, to helping me when I had internships, because back when I was an intern you would not get paid.”.

It has been revealed that llamas claims he now lives and breathes this family-first philosophy himself. The other night Llamas, who now lives in New York, anchored from the World Cup in Los Angeles and went to the game. “But then that same night, I jumped on a red eye so I could be home for a 9 AM little league game, and that's not something that that anyone has to ask me for — that's something I want to do, because I just believe that that kind of stuff needs to be automatic.”.

In a recent development, this Father’s Day, Llamas has a message for all the dads out there: “It is the best job in the world to be a father [but] give yourself some grace cause it's really tough out there. There's a lot of books and opinions and podcasts and all kinds of things that are trying to tell people how to [parent] and I think, you know, just enjoy your time with your kids. Because it goes by very fast, and I truly think the greatest thing in the world is to be a dad.”.

Industry News: Yes, My Toddler Sleeps In Our Room. No, We Haven't Stopped Having Sex.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Before you judge me, I asked experts what young kids actually understand and if our obsession with sexual privacy is more cultural and modern than we think.
  • Industry observers note that my 3-year-old still sleeps in bed with my husband and me.
  • Recent findings suggest that to which I say: We manage just fine, thanks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Before you judge me, I asked experts what young kids actually understand and if our obsession with sexual privacy is more cultural and modern than we think.

Industry observers note that my 3-year-old still sleeps in bed with my husband and me. I like cuddling him all night, and I’ve come to accept that it’s just the kind of mom I am: the clingy co-sleeping type. When he was littler, we took safe-sleep precautions with a bassinet and all that jazz, but these days, he sleeps right up next to me. Most non-co-sleeping families cringe at this. And then they immediately want to know: So how do you get intimate with your partner?

Recent findings suggest that to which I say: We manage just fine, thanks. But lately, I’ve been wondering about the elephant in the room. Or, should I say, the toddler.

According to recent reports, my husband and I NEVER have sex in the bed with our toddler. But we do sneak into the bathroom. Or sometimes, once he’s deeply asleep, we pull out a cot on the other side of the room and get it on in the dark. I’m embarrassed even admitting that.

I also don’t believe we’re the only parents who have ever found themselves in this predicament.

Here’s the thing... our house isn’t huge. And between the 3-year-old sleeping soundly in our blacked-out bedroom and one of our much more aware older kids wandering out of their rooms, we’ve chosen the former.

In a recent development, which brings me to something else we really need to address. What about the “olden days”? Ma and Pa from Little House on the Prairie managed to have four babies while living in one-room log cabins and shanties. I guarantee they weren’t heading out to the barn or the outhouse every time they wanted to have sex, especially when bears and wolves were roaming around, and temperatures dipped below zero.

Besides, many modern families around the world still live and sleep in shared spaces.

Industry observers note that lately I’ve wondered if being horrified by the idea of parents having sex in the same room as a sleeping child is a cultural thing. Is it so awful if they’re still very little? At what point does “they have no idea what’s happening” turn into “Mom and Dad need to find somewhere else to do this”?

We reached out to experts to answer all the questions you’ve probably been dying to know but have been way too embarrassed to ask.

Industry observers note that here’s the short answer: Parents don’t need to feel guilty about having sex in the same room as a newborn or young infant. An infant doesn’t have the “cognitive capacity to understand what sex is,” and they won’t remember or understand what’s going on, states Kimberly Resnick Anderson, LCSW, an AASECT-certified sex therapist.

Anderson does add one caveat, though. Having a baby nearby is likely to make parents more reserved and overall less expressive during sex. Over time, she says, that could potentially lead to a “more permanent shift” in how they express themselves sexually.

When does she recommend finding some privacy? Around age 1.

Once a child develops language and becomes mobile, she notes, it becomes harder to get it on, knowing the child could wake up in the middle of it.

Industry observers note that but Samantha Ridout, M.Phil., BCBA, a child development and behavioral expert, cautions against treating any birthday as a universal cutoff. No two children develop at exactly the same rate, she says, so there isn’t a magical age when a child suddenly becomes aware of what’s happening around them. Instead, parents should watch for their child’s growing alertness and awareness and set appropriate boundaries.

Sources indicate that I’ve found this to be true in my own family. We moved our older two kids out of our room quicker because they were definitely more aware than our last, who just feels more “babyish.”.

But both experts made one thing very clear: During sex, infants need to be in a separate, safe sleep space.

Let’s go back to my Ma and Pa observation for a minute, shall we?

The idea of children and adults having separate bedrooms is a relatively new phenomenon, notes Macall Gordon, a researcher and sleep coach with an undergraduate degree in anthropology who studies children’s sleep through a sociohistorical lens. She says before the lightbulb was invented, family life revolved around sunrise and sunset, with families often sleeping in shared spaces.

It has been revealed that but with electricity, adults could suddenly stay up after children went to bed, she adds. Now, children needed a “separate space to sleep” while adults stayed up. So the nursery and the crib came along. Then, she says, the layout of homes started to change, too, to include hallways connecting separate rooms. Before that, rooms were all connected to each other, so you had to go through one to get to another.

According to recent reports, to this day, however, a separate bedroom is still something of a privilege. Many families simply don’t have “extra, separate rooms,” Gordon points out, especially in big cities, where studios and lofts are common, or in cultures where extended family members may occupy additional bedrooms. “While we think of a separate room for children as the norm, it really wasn’t for most of our history,” Gordon shares.

According to recent reports, tiffany Belanger, cosleeping expert and founder of Cosleepy, claims the topic tends to divide her followers into two camps: those who will have sex in the room with a kid and those who won’t. When I described my scenario to her, she responded that floor sex while young kids are still sleeping in their parents’ bed is actually pretty common among the co-sleeping families she hears from.

You want to know if mine has woken up before.

Recent findings suggest that but rarely. He’s a really deep sleeper, and it’s only happened a few times. It’s dark, and when he did wake up, he immediately called out for me in that disoriented, half-asleep way toddlers do. We stopped immediately. The cot is also on the far side of the bed, outside his line of sight. As far as I know, he never saw or heard anything.

Recent findings suggest that will we emotionally damage our kid if he were to catch us in the act? Unlikely, Ridout states, if parents stay calm, stop immediately, tell the child they are safe, and answer their questions in a simple, non-panicky way.

But all of this still leaves me with the extremely practical question that got us into this mess in the first place.

Recent findings suggest that parents have to get creative, flexible, and spontaneous, indicates Anderson. That might mean asking family or friends to babysit when you can, doing it in other rooms, or using whatever short pockets of privacy you can find.

In a recent development, and while Belanger reassures me that my floor-sex solution isn't unheard of among co-sleeping parents, the other experts think it’s not a great option when kids become mobile and verbal. So, I suppose it might be time to retire the cot. Where to next?

#160541. How To Make Fewer Grocery Trips & Still Eat Well

How To Make Fewer Grocery Trips & Still Eat Well

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1381 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scarymommy

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Groceries cost a fortune, gas isn’t cheap… every “quick” run to the store somehow costs you 60 bucks or more.
  • Industry observers note that it’s a phenomenon that happens more often than not these days: You run into the store for milk, cheese, eggs, and a few other basics, and walk out wondering how in the hell a small handful of grocery bags just set you back upwards of 100 bucks.
  • According to recent reports, the reality is groceries are still painfully expensive, and plenty of families are stretched thinner than ever.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Groceries cost a fortune, gas isn’t cheap… every “quick” run to the store somehow costs you 60 bucks or more. Experts share how to shop less and still feed your family well.

Industry observers note that it’s a phenomenon that happens more often than not these days: You run into the store for milk, cheese, eggs, and a few other basics, and walk out wondering how in the hell a small handful of grocery bags just set you back upwards of 100 bucks. Worse, you then have to play budget Tetris, moving money around to make sure you have funds for the inevitable grocery run you’ll have to make next week. Add in the gas it takes to get to and from, and you’re spent literally and figuratively.

According to recent reports, the reality is groceries are still painfully expensive, and plenty of families are stretched thinner than ever. And, sure, cutting back on trips is probably one of the easiest and most logical ways to save money (and time, and sanity). But it begs the question: How long can you go between grocery runs without your family surviving on cereal benders?

We asked food and budgeting experts how they personally make it work.

Industry observers note that most of the experts we polled remarked one big shop a week is sort of the sweet spot. “Every extra trip not only takes up valuable time, but is also another chance to grab things that aren’t on the list and drive up your overall grocery bill,” states Laurie Hise, CEO of Passionate Penny Pincher.

In a recent development, is it possible to stretch it to every two weeks? Maybe. But AJ Prasaguet, head of the iconic Palace bar and restaurant in Miami Beach, points out that biweekly shopping “can work if you have the storage space, freezer capacity, and money available upfront. Those are real considerations, and not every household has all three.”.

In a recent development, amber Hanson, a licensed nutritionist and founder of Whole You Nutrition, emphasizes that there’s no cut-and-dry, one-size-fits-all answer. Your ideal grocery-shopping cadence will ultimately depend on things like how close you live to a store and when your paycheck hits the bank. If you get paid every two weeks, it might make sense to shop on that timeframe too.

It has been revealed that before you make your little grocery list and head to the store, open up your own fridge, freezer, and pantry. “The best way to save money is to use what you have already paid for,” says Hanson.

Jenn Lueke, Latest York Times-bestselling author of Don’t Think About Dinner, does her inventory every Friday night, then builds the next week’s meals around what’s left. Example: “If I know I have a half carton of broth that needs to be used, I’ll make sure to pick up a grain, like rice or quinoa, that I can cook in it.”.

It has been revealed that prasaguet goes one step further. “Give an ingredient its next job before you buy it. If a recipe needs half a container of something, decide where the other half is going.” Take cabbage, for instance. It can be slaw one night, stir-fry the next, and soup filler after that.

Another tip Hise is a fan of is ordering online for pickup or delivery when you can. The simple act of skipping the aisles means you don't have to worry about impulse buys wreaking havoc on your total.

As a busy working mom who regularly feels she has to have everything for the week figured out at all times, this was very liberating to hear! As the experts remind us, life happens. Looks change. A rigid seven-night menu is a fast track to wasted food.

Recent findings suggest that but if it makes you feel better to have the week mostly lined up, you could follow Hise’s example: plan five “fresh” dinners a week, leaving one night for leftovers and one for a meal pulled from what’s already in the pantry, fridge, or freezer. Prasaguet relies on a similar formula: four planned dinners, one leftovers meal, one pantry or freezer dinner, on flex night. “That gives the week some structure without pretending everything will go according to plan,” he says.

Recent findings suggest that lueke recommends starting with dinners, then exploring how you can make the most of them. “Will the slow-cooker chicken stretch to cover lunches for half the week too? Can I make a double batch of quinoa and bulk up our mid-week sheet pan dinner?” Theme nights like Taco Tuesday or Breakfast for Dinner also help reduce decision fatigue.

According to recent reports, the trick to making groceries last, many of the pros explained, is buying foods with different lifespans and eating them in the right order. “You do not want an entire cart of produce that all needs attention at once,” emphasizes Prasaguet.

Lueke thinks about it in three zones:.

Recent findings suggest that andrea Woroch, a consumer savings expert, notes that some hardy produce (think garlic, potatoes, sweet potatoes, winter squash, even whole apples) can last for months depending on storage conditions as well as how they’re handled. For fast-spoilers like berries, resist the urge to buy the giant fresh packs unless you know your family will gobble them down. Otherwise, stock up on frozen.

If you're afraid frozen and canned food won't pack the same nutritional punch as fresh, well, the experts beg to differ.

According to recent reports, “One of the biggest misconceptions about healthy eating is that fresh foods are always better than frozen or canned alternatives. That’s simply not the case,” indicates Jennifer Pallian, a registered dietitian and founder of Foodess. Frozen vegetables are typically flash-frozen shortly after harvest, and research has found they can be just as nutritious as fresh produce that’s been sitting in your fridge for several days. In some cases, they even have more vitamin C.”.

Don’t turn your nose up at canned staples, either. Pallian is a substantial proponent of canned light tuna (a solid source of protein, selenium, and omega-3s) and canned chickpeas, which pack both protein and fiber and are already cooked.

Just opt for low-sodium or no-salt-added canned veggies and beans, and be mindful of foods packed in juices, syrups, or sauces.

Adopting a few little habits can go a long way toward making food last until your next grocery run:.

However, Prasaguet reminds us, “Stretching groceries should never mean stretching food safety.” That means refrigerating leftovers within two hours, eating them within three to four days, or sticking them in the freezer.

Industry observers note that you should know that eating well doesn’t mean you have to buy a bunch of fancy superfoods. “Some of the most nutrient-dense foods in the grocery store are also the cheapest,” Hanson states.

Here’s what our experts say they keep stocked:.

And while many of us think shopping in bulk must save money, Prasaguet notes that it’s “only better value if you can afford it, store it, and finish it.” Hise’s workaround is to grab a few extra cans whenever they’re on sale. “A few extra cans a month can add up to a pantry that carries you through a tight month.”.

If you feel like a failure every time you serve your family dinner out of a bag or can, it’s high time you cut yourself some slack.

Industry observers note that “Frozen and canned foods that you actually eat beat fresh vegetables you throw away every time,” says Hise. Link agrees, adding, “I’d much rather see a family use convenient foods they enjoy than buy fresh ingredients that become a science experiment in the crisper drawer.”.

Recent findings suggest that “A fed family is a win, and ‘fresh’ isn’t the measure of a good dinner," Lueke puts it simply. A balanced meal is made up of a protein, a plant or two, and something filling. It truly does not matter if those came from the produce section or the freezer aisle.

Industry observers note that but maybe Prasaguet sums it up best. “You do not have to prove your love through a complicated dinner,” he reassures. “Feeding your family with the resources you have is already an act of care.”.

#160539. How To Have A Lazy Thanksgiving Without Losing That Holiday Magic

How To Have A Lazy Thanksgiving Without Losing That Holiday Magic

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1037 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scarymommy

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Delegate the sides, veto the cranberry sauce, and actually sit down at your own table.
  • Industry observers note that as a child, I remember the holiday season feeling like the most magical time of the year.
  • It has been revealed that who decorated the house like that?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Delegate the sides, veto the cranberry sauce, and actually sit down at your own table.

Industry observers note that as a child, I remember the holiday season feeling like the most magical time of the year. Thanksgiving, in particular, seemed like a massive deal because it meant Christmas was right around the corner. The house always felt so warm and cozy with fall decorations on full display — their last hurrah before Christmas took over. And the food. There was always so much delicious food to consume. It was wonderful. It was special. And now, as an adult, I realize it was all thanks to... my mom.

It has been revealed that who decorated the house like that? Mom. Who invited the guests and organized the whole Thanksgiving affair? Mom. Who made all of that yummy food? You guessed it — Mom! For me, all of that stuff just seemed to magically get done without much fuss. But there was a fuss. And it wasn’t magic. It was Mom. And now that I’m a mom myself, I realize just how much she had on her plate, figuratively speaking. (Literally, she probably didn’t have much on her plate at all because she was too busy hosting to actually enjoy the meal she created.).

The point is, Thanksgiving can prove to be such a stressful time for moms with all the planning and cooking and putting everyone else’s needs above their own. So much effort is put into making this day perfect for everyone but themselves. But moms deserve to enjoy this holiday too, which is why I say it’s time to invoke a upcoming tradition known as the Lazy Thanksgiving.

According to recent reports, now I know what you’re thinking, but don’t let the name fool you; a Lazy Thanksgiving doesn’t mean a Lame Thanksgiving. There are still plenty of ways to make this day feel special without completely wiping yourself out in the process. Here’s how.

Even if you’re hosting Thanksgiving dinner, that doesn’t mean you should automatically carry the load of the entire meal on your shoulders. Do what any good boss does and delegate an assortment of dishes to other members of the family for them to bring over on the day of. If there’s one thing that you personally enjoy making, then by all means have at it. But everything else should be outsourced to others. Don’t let the burden fall solely on you.

Industry observers note that to add a fun twist, reveal that anyone who contributes a dish gets their name entered into a raffle for a special prize at the end of the night. This could be something hassle-free and small, like a cute little ornament or a goodie bag of chocolate. This not only serves as a great incentive to help lighten your cooking load, but it also gives the winner a sweet keepsake of the occasion. (It’s worth noting that this prize part is completely optional — no family member should need to be bribed to help out.).

It has been revealed that if you don’t feel comfortable with a potluck approach, but still feel overwhelmed at the thought of making so many dishes, feel free to just simply not make some of those items. (Think of it as a food-ocracy and you’re the president.) Cranberry sauce may be thought of as a Thanksgiving staple, but if only a spoonful or so gets eaten each year, then you are well within your rights to take it off the menu. The same goes for squash or yams or anything else that never ends up feeling worth the effort you put into making it. Odds are, no one is going to care or miss it, and those who do obtain the right to make it themselves.

Industry observers note that if you really want to unburden yourself and maximize your relaxation time, you could always get the food from somewhere else and either pick it up or have it delivered right to your door. Honey Baked is always a solid option with great choices for a delicious holiday feast.

According to recent reports, it’s more expensive than making it yourself, but a lot less time-consuming, and if various family members chip in to make it happen, it could end up being more than worth the cost. That way you can sit down and actually have time to enjoy everyone’s firm for a change.

Do you enjoy cooking but dread the massive clean-up job that comes at the end of it all? Trade in regular dishes and cups for paper ones. Sure, there will still be some dishes to contend with that the actual food was cooked in, but this swap definitely helps cut down on the task and leaves extra room for everything else to go in the dishwasher.

Sources indicate that as a bonus, you can make use of all the extra paper plates by turning it into a fun craft competition for the kids. Whether they use them to make a snowman or some Thanksgiving-inspired creation, this is a great way to get their artistic juices flowing. Choose a family member to be the judge and give out a prize to the winner each year: something like a small toy or maybe even a NeeDoh if you really want the crowd to go wild and can get your hands on one. The kids will love the challenge and look forward to it as part of an annual tradition.

Then again, do you want to go completely rogue? Throw tradition out the window and order takeout or make an easy casserole that will feed everyone and involve zero stress. No turkey. No stuffing. No gravy. No hassle.

According to recent reports, however you choose to invoke your “Lazy Thanksgiving,” just make sure that it’s the right fit for you. The whole point is to put less pressure on this day, and by extension, yourself. Remember that less work for you doesn’t equate to a less enjoyable time for everyone else. You being around more, instead of running back and forth to the kitchen, is something the whole family will be thankful for in the long run.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

From activewear to snacks to the crucial stuff we all forget about, here’s your complete product guide to the gear your young athlete needs.

Industry observers note that back-to-school season does not just mean notebooks, lunch boxes, and the shoes your kid insists everyone else already has. If your kid plays sports, it also means damp socks wedged into the back seat, a gym bag that smells like evidence, water bottles with no lids, and a towel that is wet, rank, and somehow still in use.

Most young athletes need the same basic stuff, no matter what they play: a sturdy water bottle, sweat-ready clothes, socks that do not quit, sunscreen, towels, deodorant, recovery gear, and something to contain the mess. Nothing here is precious. Nothing is so sport-specific that it only works for one season. This is the Amazon gear parents end up buying anyway, pulled together before the season takes over the sports bag, the laundry room, and your will to live.

In a recent development, A good water bottle is the first thing every young athlete needs, and the first thing they will leave on a bench somewhere. Look for one that is durable, easy to clean, and big enough to get them through practice.

Recent findings suggest that the 50-ounce size gives kids enough water for long practices and tournament days, and the tethered leakproof cap means one less loose lid rolling around the car. It is also lightweight, clippable, and dishwasher-safe, which matters because no parent needs another thing that requires special handling.

Industry observers note that some practices are long, hot, and sweaty enough that water alone may not cut it. A sports drink can help replace electrolytes when sweat is doing most of the work.

In a recent development, this variety pack has electrolytes, with no added sugar and no artificial sweeteners, flavors, or dyes. At 20 calories per bottle, it is a lighter sports-drink option for parents who want hydration help without sending a kid into practice with something that looks like melted candy.

Recent findings suggest that some sports days run straight through the normal eating schedule, which is how kids end up starving in the car and furious at everyone. A protein bar is useful before practice, after practice, or between games, but check school rules and allergens before tossing one into a team bag.

According to recent reports, this 10-count variety pack has flavors built around chocolate, peanut butter, blueberry, fruit, and nuts. The bars are gluten-free, made with simple ingredients, and have 12 grams of protein per bar, but some contain common allergens including eggs, peanuts, almonds, and cashews.

It has been revealed that fall sports still mean sun exposure. A sweat-resistant sunscreen belongs in every sports bag, especially for after-school practices, weekend tournaments and kids who swear they “don’t burn.”.

This sunscreen is fast-absorbing, nongreasy, and water- and sweat-resistant for up to 80 minutes, which makes it a practical fit for practices and games. Supergoop is made for face and body, so kids do not need separate bottles.

Industry observers note that A school backpack is already doing too much. A dedicated sports bag gives clothes, towels, water bottles, deodorant, and gear somewhere to live that is not the floor of your car.

This has a spacious main compartment for school and practice gear, plus a ventilated shoe compartment to keep wet sneakers or cleats away from clean clothes and tech. The water-resistant base is the quiet win here, because locker room floors, wet fields, and rainy parking lots are not kind to regular backpacks.

Industry observers note that wet socks, damp towels, and postpractice clothes should not touch anything clean. A wet-dry bag keeps the gross stuff contained until someone remembers laundry exists.

These bags are technically built for diapers, swimsuits, and day care messes, which is exactly why it works for youth sports. The 12.5-by-16-inch size, washable fabric, heat-sealed seams, and leak-resistant design make it useful for wet socks, damp towels, and gear you do not want touching anything else.

Cotton is fine until it turns into a wet dish towel with sleeves. A moisture-wicking shirt helps kids stay more comfortable through practice, conditioning, and the ride home.

In a recent development, the quick-drying fabric wicks sweat and dries fast, which is the whole point of a practice shirt. It is soft enough for school or general wear too, so it does not become another piece of gear that only gets used once a week.

Recent findings suggest that every young athlete needs shorts that can handle sweat, dirt, turf, and repeated washing. They should be light, easy to move in, and not so expensive that losing one pair becomes a family event.

Industry observers note that the listing calls these soccer shorts, but the sweat-wicking Climacool fabric, adjustable drawcord waist, and recycled polyester interlock make them useful for more than one sport. They are built for movement and repeated washing, which is what matters.

Bad underwear can ruin a practice faster than bad weather. Athletic underwear should move, breathe, and stay put under uniforms, shorts, and base layers without bunching, pinching, or becoming the thing your kid complains about the entire ride home.

These have a 5-inch inseam, a wide soft waistband, a breathable athletic feel, and flatlock seams for durability. The contoured pouch and tagless back make them a practical under-uniform option for boys who need support without bulk.

These are made with smooth stretch fabric, a seamless waistband, and a tag-free design to help reduce irritation during school, sports, and everyday movement. The lightweight performance fabric gives active kids a flexible fit without pinching, digging, or bunching under gear.

A hoodie is the unofficial uniform of kids waiting before games, riding home after practice, or denying they are cold.

This is a straightforward school-to-practice hoodie with a relaxed fit, kangaroo pocket, thumbholes, and midweight fabric. It is the kind of layer kids can wear constantly without making you nervous every time it leaves the house.

Industry observers note that A base layer helps with sweat, coverage, and comfort without adding bulk. It works under jerseys, hoodies, and uniforms when the weather cannot decide to be seasonally appropriate.

In a recent development, this long-sleeve top is made with lightweight HeatGear fabric that wicks sweat and dries fast, with mesh panels for ventilation and flatlock seams for easier movement. It is not a heavy thermal layer, but that is why it works for school sports: Kids can wear it under gear without overheating five minutes into warm-ups.

Socks disappear faster than almost anything else in a young athlete’s life. Buy more than seems reasonable, because wet, thin, or blister-making socks can wreck a practice fast.

These socks use a combed cotton and polyester blend with spandex for stretch, which means they are built to breathe, hold their shape, and survive repeated washing. The medium cushioning and reinforced heels and toes make them a practical everyday pick for kids who burn through socks like it is part of the sport.

Slides give kids something easy to wear before and after games, especially when cleats are muddy, socks are wet, or feet need a break. They also make locker rooms, pools, and postpractice errands less gross.

Industry observers note that these slides use OOfoam, which the brand states absorbs 37% more impact than traditional footwear foams. The closed-cell foam is machine-washable and designed to minimize odor, which makes it perfect for locker rooms, postgame errands, and the ride home.

Recent findings suggest that A quick-dry towel works for sweat, rain, swimming, muddy legs, and the towel situation no parent wants to inspect. It dries faster than a regular bath towel, which matters when it gets forgotten in a bag overnight.

The listing claims it absorbs five times its own weight and dries fast when hung by the snap loop. It also packs into a ventilated carry bag, which makes it easier to keep in a sports bag than a bulky bath towel from home.

A sports bag becomes a swamp fast. Packing cubes give clean clothes, extra socks, base layers, and small gear a fighting chance of staying together instead of becoming part of the bottom-of-the-bag sludge.

These packing cubes keep clean backup clothes, socks, and small gear organized inside a sports bag, backpack or a duffel. The Del Dia colors are random and one-of-a-kind, which means no two sets look the same, and your kid has a chance — albeit small — of recognizing their own stuff.

Youth sports shoes can turn toxic fast, especially when they live in a bag between practices. A shoe deodorizer helps keep sneakers, cleats, and slides from stinking up the car, mudroom, or whatever corner your kid has claimed for gear.

Recent findings suggest that these compact deodorizers are built for shoes, gym bags, lockers, and sports gear, so they do not just solve one stink problem. The twist-to-activate design lets kids control the scent level, assuming they remember to use these before the shoes become a family issue.

According to recent reports, some sports smells do not come out in the wash because the offending item never goes in the wash. A gear spray helps with helmets, gloves, pads, bags, and other equipment that gets sweaty, rank, and somehow keeps getting used.

It has been revealed that this spray deodorizes sports equipment, including helmets, gloves, bags, pads and gym gear, and the brand indicates it works for everything from football and hockey to lacrosse, soccer, volleyball, and boxing. It only requires a spray-and-air-dry routine, which is about as much cleaning as most sports families can promise on a weeknight.

Keep one in the sports bag, one at home, and maybe one in the car, because youth sports have a way of exposing every deodorant failure.

In a recent development, this deodorant is dermatologically tested and made for young, sensitive skin, which makes sense for kids who are just starting to need it. It is designed to protect against body odor without using a grown-up scent that confirms itself from across the room.

In a recent development, sometimes there is no shower. Body wipes help kids clean up enough to survive the car ride, dinner, homework or whatever comes next.

These individually wrapped 8-by-10-inch wipes are made for the exact no-shower problem sports families know well. They are hypoallergenic, paraben-free, and alcohol-free, and include aloe vera and vitamin E, so they are a practical bag staple for postpractice cleanup.

According to recent reports, fields, gyms, locker rooms, and portable bathrooms are not exactly sterile environments. Hand sanitizer is small, cheap, and useful before snacks, after bathroom runs, and after handling shared gear.

This unscented trio gives you three travel-friendly sanitizer sprays, which is useful if you want one for the sports bag, one for the car, and one that will disappear immediately.

Sunscreen, deodorant, lip balm, wipes, hair ties, and sanitizer should not be rolling loose at the bottom of a sports bag. A small toiletry bag keeps the tiny essentials together and makes them easier to find.

This zip pouch has internal mesh pockets and a separate compartment, so the small stuff has a fighting chance of staying organized. The swivel hook is useful for hanging it in a locker, on a backpack or anywhere that is not the bottom of a filthy sports bag.

According to recent reports, lips burn too, and kids almost never think about it. SPF lip balm is small enough to live in a bag and useful for long days outside.

This three-pack has SPF 30 and includes aloe and vitamin E to help protect and moisturize lips. The multi-pack is useful because lip balm has the life expectancy of a loose sock.

Industry observers note that late-summer and fall practices can come with mosquitoes, especially on fields near grass, water, or woods. Bug spray keeps kids from spending half of practice swatting instead of playing.

This spray repels mosquitoes, ticks, and biting flies, and the misting design gives more even coverage than the panic-spray method most kids use.

It has been revealed that hair ties vanish, break, and somehow become community property. Keep extras in the sports bag for any kid who needs hair out of their face, whether they play rec soccer or want to look like Norway’s Erling Haaland before warm-ups.

These hair ties are designed to flex with different hair thicknesses and hold without pinching or pulling. They are also made to minimize breakage, which matters when a kid is ripping out a ponytail in the car after practice.

It has been revealed that fall sports do not stop because the weather is annoying. A lightweight rain jacket gives kids real coverage for wet practices, sidelines, and the long walk from field to car.

In a recent development, this waterproof nylon shell is light enough to layer but protective enough for everything from drizzle to a sudden downpour. It has a hood, two hand pockets, elastic cuffs, and reflective detail, which makes it a practical all-season piece for kids who will absolutely claim they are fine while visibly getting soaked.

Something will hurt. A reusable ice pack is useful for bumps, sore knees, rolled ankles, and the ride home after a hard practice.

These reusable gel packs stay flexible out of the freezer, so they can wrap around knees, ankles and other hard-to-ice spots. The included soft cover adds a barrier between the cold pack and skin, which makes it easier to use in the car or on the couch after practice.

Reusable ice packs only help if someone remembered the freezer. Instant cold packs belong in a sports bag or tournament kit for away games and minor sideline injuries.

According to recent reports, these single-use cold packs activate after folding, so parents do not need a freezer, cooler, or advance planning to get cold therapy on the sideline. They are designed to reach 32 degrees Fahrenheit, which is exactly the point.

It has been revealed that athletic tape is the thing nobody thinks about until someone needs it immediately. It can help with sore knees, cranky ankles, tight shoulders and small body complaints that show up five minutes before warmups.

It has been revealed that this 16-foot roll can be cut to size, so parents are not locked into one strip length for every kid, joint, or complaint. It is breathable, hypoallergenic, and latex-free, and it’s designed to stay on for one to three days through sweat, showers, and weather, while still allowing a range of motion.

New shoes, wet socks, and long tournament days can turn a small hot spot into a full limp. Blister bandages take up almost no room and can save a practice, game or long ride home.

It has been revealed that these hydrocolloid bandages cushion blisters, cuts, and scrapes while helping protect them from water, dirt and germs. They are waterproof and designed to stay on for up to five days, which is useful when a kid’s heel is already angry and the season has no interest in pausing.

Youth sports produces scrapes, turf burns, mystery cuts, and dramatic reactions to minor blood. A small first-aid kit should have bandages, antiseptic wipes, gauze, and the basics you need before anyone starts searching the glove compartment for a napkin.

This compact hardcase packs 120 supplies, including adhesive bandages, butterfly closures, gauze pads, alcohol prep pads, antiseptic wipes, sting relief pads, gloves, tweezers, scissors, and medical tape. It is slim enough to fit in a backpack, glove box, or sports bag, but stocked well enough for the everyday cuts, scrapes, and minor injuries that come with kids playing hard.

This is the most sport-specific item on the list. It matters for football, lacrosse, field hockey, basketball, martial arts, wrestling, and other sports in which player contact, falls, elbows, or sticks can impact teeth.

This boil-and-bite mouthguard molds to the teeth for a more custom fit and is made with shock-absorbing EVA material to help protect teeth, gums, and jaw during contact sports. The slim profile, airflow vents, and optional strap version make it more practical for kids who need protection but still have to breathe, talk, and keep it in place.

According to recent reports, if it is not labeled, it is a donation to the lost-and-found economy. Name labels help water bottles, hoodies, towels, bags, shoes, and gear make their way back before another parent takes home the same black sweatshirt.

This 114-label pack includes stick-on clothing labels, shoe labels, large and small rectangle labels, and bag tags, so parents can mark almost everything that leaves the house. The labels are peel-and-stick, waterproof and laundry-safe, which matters when the gear is sweaty, wet, washed constantly, or lost somewhere between the field and the car.

Long practices, races, meets, and tournament days can turn kids into empty tanks fast. Energy chews are quick, portable fuel for older kids who need carbs they can eat fast without digging through a bag for whatever got crushed at the bottom.

These chews have 23 grams of carbs per serving. They are organic, include sodium to help replenish electrolytes after exercise, and are easier to stash in a gym bag than a full-size snack.

Industry observers note that warm-up pants used to mean joggers, but kids have moved on. Wide-leg sweatpants are the more current version: loose; comfortable; and useful before practice, after practice, or on the ride home.

In a recent development, these have an elastic waist, pockets, and a wide-leg cut that feels more current than basic warm-ups. The fabric is lightweight, soft, breathable, and slightly stretchy, which makes these useful for school, practice, running around, and the postgame outfit change your kid suddenly cares about.

It has been revealed that these have a straight, wide-leg cut, letter print, and loose, trendy fit that works with hoodies, jackets and sweatshirts. They are made for daily wear, workouts, sports, running, and outdoor activities, which puts them in the exact lane between warm-up pants and “my kid will actually wear these.”.

It has been revealed that this is not performance gear. This is for the kid who walks off the field sweaty, red-faced, and suddenly needs to fix their hair before anyone is allowed to leave the parking lot.

It adds grip before styling, which should help with the sacred ritual of fixing the hair before anyone is allowed to leave the parking lot. Postgame vanity is real, and frankly, it may be the most consistent part of youth sports.

19 Gifts For Moms Who Just Want To Sit The F Down

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2018 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scarymommy

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Give her a little something that encourages her to enjoy a few minutes of peace (and zero responsibility).
  • Industry observers note that most of us aren’t going to turn our noses up at a pretty piece of jewelry or say no to a spa day.
  • While we love our families fiercely, sometimes we really do just need a tiny breather to collect ourselves.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Give her a little something that encourages her to enjoy a few minutes of peace (and zero responsibility).

Industry observers note that most of us aren’t going to turn our noses up at a pretty piece of jewelry or say no to a spa day. But if you really get to the heart of what most moms want, it’s pretty simple: to sit the f*ck down. Just for a minute. Maybe with a warm drink that we don’t have to reheat three times, maybe under a cozy blanket, definitely without someone saying “Mom? Mom? Mom” every 12 seconds (go ask your father).

While we love our families fiercely, sometimes we really do just need a tiny breather to collect ourselves. Or to stare blankly at the wall. So, if you’re shopping for a mom who is always moving and doing and running on fumes, think about gifting her something from this list. Hopefully, they’ll help her slow down, relax, and finally — finally — take a moment for herself.

Every exhausted mom deserves at least one deeply luxurious blanket, and Cocoon has a reputation for being that girl. It’s a bit of a splurge, which makes it the perfect gift for the mom in your life who loves to snuggle up but rarely treats herself. I fell hard for this new Hydrangea Stripe colorway the minute I saw it. The muted sage, cream, olive, and ochre stripes are cozy and elevated enough to leave draped on the couch all year long. It has such a dreamy vintage aesthetic to it! I’m literally cuddled in it right now and couldn’t be happier. — Julie Sprankles, Deputy Editor, Lifestyle & Entertainment.

According to recent reports, for the mom who has forgotten what it feels like to sit down, this kit turns a two-minute ritual into a legitimate excuse to stop moving, with a face dry brush, a body dry brush, a body healing oil, and an instruction card that walks you through the whole thing. Dry brushing is a slow, grounding routine that exfoliates your skin and gets your circulation going, and following it with the oil makes it feel like a mini spa moment in your own bathroom. It’s a self-care gift that comes with built-in permission to take a breather, and I use mine as the one quiet part of my day that’s just for me! — Katie Garrity, Senior Editor, News & Social.

Recent findings suggest that I have no idea why, but I carry so much tension in my feet! By the end of the day, after my feet have logged what feels like 100 miles, I relish sitting down and sliding them into this warming foot massager. It has soft, fleece-lined pockets that feel so good, especially when you flip on the heat. I also really like that it has two vibration levels (though I keep mine cranked to the highest). — Julie Sprankles.

According to recent reports, for the mom who’s been on her feet since 6 a.m. and has finally earned the right to sit down, these socks are the reward that starts working before you hit the couch. The light compression (13 to 16 mmHg) is mapped across 11 targeted zones around the arch and ankle, so your feet feel supported without that suffocating squeeze, and the cushioned sole, seamless toe, and breathable mesh make them feel like a hug for your feet. They come in a 3-pack of organic cotton, they stay put in your shoes, and they’re the gift that claims “you’ve earned this, now go sit down”! — Katie Garrity.

Recent findings suggest that this is my new end-of-day best friend! I slip it on, lean back, and let it work its magic while one of its nine built-in Headspace meditations talks me down from the day. The motor is super quiet, which is nice, and the targeted compression and heat just kind of melt away any tension. I have a really hard time carving out any downtime for myself, so I appreciate that this makes it easy for me to ignore the world for 15 minutes. — Julie Sprankles.

Sources indicate that for the mom who spends her whole day bending, lifting, and carrying everyone else, this wearable back pad is the gift that finally gives her a reason to sit down for 20 minutes. It combines red light, near-infrared light, and eight vibration points in a cordless wrap you strap on with a remote, so she can sit, scroll, or stare at the wall while it works on her lower back. It’s definitely a splurge, but it’s the kind of gift that gives her something money rarely buys: a guilt-free break! — Katie Garrity.

My ideal day of rest most certainly involves curling up in a comfy spot with a snuggly blanket and a good book, with a candle flickering for ambiance. I could not ask for a better way to complete that fantasy than this Wonderwick Smells Like Rhysand candle. It’s inspired by how Feyre describes Rhys’s scent in A Court of Mist and Fury: think rain and sea salt and hints of citrus. Every scent by this brand is pulled straight from pages, which is peak bookish nerdery. This one has a “mated pair” (Feyre, natch) designed to smell great together. IYKYK. — Julie Sprankles.

Sources indicate that A gorgeous puzzle is a great way to steal a few minutes because your kids will be totally enraptured. Completing the Puzzle is brilliant because it’s the first-ever puzzle rental subscription where you can order high-quality puzzles, have them delivered to your door, and, well, basically have something guaranteed to keep your kid distracted for a little chunk of time every month. — Kate Auletta, Editor in Chief.

If you’re a mom whose coffee goes cold the second you sit down, this tumbler is the fix: double-wall insulation keeps your drink hot or cold for hours, so it’s still perfect by the time you actually get to relax. The handle makes it easy to carry from room to room, the quarter-turn straw lid keeps spills at bay, and the shape fits in a car cup holder, so it goes everywhere you do. It’s the cup I keep at arm’s reach on the couch, which is exactly where a mom who finally sits down wants it. — Katie Garrity.

Want true peace and quiet? The noise cancellation on these headphones is next level. They block out everything, and the immersive audio spatializes sound so it literally feels like the music is happening right in front of you. Super comfortable, they’re designed for long listening sessions, which you’ll undoubtedly enjoy thanks to all kinds of cool settings and customization options. — Julie Sprankles.

Recent findings suggest that A candle that comes with a built-in reason to stop moving feels like exactly what I need, since lighting it is basically a signal to the whole house that Mom is sitting down. It’s a tall, hand-rolled candle made with organic beeswax and soy wax, covered in hibiscus, rose petals, and lavender, and inspired by a traditional Mesoamerican healing ritual. The set comes with two candles that burn for about two hours each, so it’s a $36 permission slip to light one, sit down, and do absolutely nothing! — Katie Garrity.

Recent findings suggest that the name doesn’t lie: These DSG So Soft Wide Leg Pants really are SO SOFT. They’re a silky, lightweight fleece with a high-rise waist and a relaxed wide-leg fit... so basically the perfect uniform for a mom in relaxation mode. As a tall girlie (almost 5’10”), I’m thrilled by the fact that they come in a long length, and that they’re polished enough to wear out and about too. — Julie Sprankles.

The black spruce, sweet cinnamon, and vanilla scent of this limited-edition candle is exactly what I’d light right before I finally sit down on the couch with a coffee and refuse to get back up. It comes in a recyclable glass jar and burns for about 25 hours in the medium size and 35 in the large, which should get you through the whole season of sitting down! — Katie Garrity.

Recent findings suggest that if you think a self-heating eye mask makes so much sense, well, for starters, it definitely does. But also, that tracks since a new (and also tired) mom created the brand with others like her in mind. The result is these beautifully packaged, individually wrapped eye masks that gently melt away tension around your eyes. The sandalwood scent is so divine, and at $30 for a set of five, they make such a great little affordable luxury gift. — Julie Sprankles.

Sources indicate that I have a chronic illness that causes high inflammation, skin challenges, and a whole host of other things... and one of the biggest game-changers for me in the last few years has been red light therapy. Bonus: It requires you to sit down and rest for a few minutes! I don’t have room for a giant full-body panel in my house, so I love that the Helios-300 is a compact desktop panel. I set it up in my home office and take little breaks throughout the week to bask like a lizard. You can run the red and near-infrared lights separately or together and aim them at your face, neck, or whatever’s feeling achy or needs a little TLC. — Julie Sprankles.

According to recent reports, when the kids are finally in bed and I have earned the right to sit down, these are what I reach for, because it’s dry rosé with sparkling water and a hint of natural fruit flavor in a 12-ounce can that’s only 100 calories and 4.5% ABV. They come in Strawberry Peach and Blackberry Lemon, in 4-packs or an 8-count variety pack, so you can find your favorite without opening a whole bottle of wine. — Katie Garrity.

In a recent development, my god, these slippers are so unbelievably cozy and warm. The ankle collar can be worn high or folded down, and the soles are sturdy, so you can wear them for quick trips outside, too (it’s nice to be able to wear these to keep my feet warm lounging around inside, but also to walk out to the mailbox). Definitely follow the sizing instructions to make sure you get the right fit — once you do, you’ll be a fan for life. What makes me feel even better about wearing mine is Minnetonka’s dedication to sustainability and their ongoing work with Native American communities, including funding education, supporting Native artisans, and investing in organizations that preserve and uplift Indigenous culture. — Julie Sprankles.

I feel like a proper grown-up now because I finally got a robot vacuum to take one of the most relentless chores off my plate. The bObsweep Maxim vacuums AND mops, powering through pet hair... a huge need in my house, as I have a 100-lb rescue husky who sheds like nobody’s business. It maps my house by itself, and the extendable brushes and mop arms reach right into corners and along baseboards. Also a pro: It knows to stop mopping when it hits a rug! It’s a major-ticket item, but it genuinely makes my life so much easier. — Julie Sprankles.

This mask is the closest thing I have to a legitimate reason to sit down, because a 20-minute session means I’m lying on the couch with it on and nobody can ask me for anything. Literally, my kids are scared of me when I wear it, so they leave me alone. It’s cordless with a wireless remote, so you can wander around the house if you want to, and it has four color modes (red, blue, orange, and purple), each paired with near-infrared light, plus 5, 10, or 20-minute timer settings. The soft, flexible silicone is comfortable enough to wear while you do absolutely nothing, which makes it a skincare splurge and a forced break in one. — Katie Garrity.
