10 Times Ted Lasso Totally Nailed This Whole Parenting Thing

📅 15 Jul 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2064 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fatherly

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that ted Lasso isn’t the perfect father, but he’s one who can teach us a thing...
  • Way back in 2020, when I heard that Apple TV was releasing a Ted Lasso show based on the NBC Sports English Premier League promo campaign of the same name, I dismissed the concept out of hand.
  • Recent findings suggest that here’s the thing I failed to anticipate: Ted Lasso is, at its core, a show about fatherhood.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that ted Lasso isn’t the perfect father, but he’s one who can teach us a thing... or 10.

Way back in 2020, when I heard that Apple TV was releasing a Ted Lasso show based on the NBC Sports English Premier League promo campaign of the same name, I dismissed the concept out of hand. Sure, I loved the cheeky ads where an American football coach goes to England to manage a football club. But the premise felt too thin to flesh out into a full series, and Jason Sudeikis’ body of work up to that point didn’t inspire confidence that a sitcom based on the character could hold my attention.

I couldn’t have been more wrong.

Recent findings suggest that here’s the thing I failed to anticipate: Ted Lasso is, at its core, a show about fatherhood. Not in a neat, Hallmark-movie kind of way, but in the messy, long-distance, guilt-soaked, love-you-so-much-it-hurts way that a lot of us actually live it. Ted’s relationship with his son, Henry — conducted mostly through grainy FaceTime calls across a six-hour time difference — is the quiet beating heart of all three seasons.

While the rest of AFC Richmond is arguing about formations and tabloid covers, Ted is trying to figure out how to be a good dad from 4,000 miles away while working through how his relationship with his own father has formed him.

According to recent reports, the man is not perfect. Nobody raising kids is, and running off to London without your family to accept a job you’re wholly unqualified for as an act of emotional avoidance is a narrative necessity, but it’s a flaw many folks have pointed out.

But along the way, he does his best and makes the right plays in the moments that count. And since parenting lessons wrapped inside a feel-good soccer comedy are my personal favorite delivery mechanism, let’s run through 10 times Ted Lasso gave us a genuine master class in this whole dad thing.

It’s Ted’s first night in London. He’s jet-lagged and disoriented, and the very first thing he does is call home to Henry. He fumbles the time zones and sounds a little lost, but he makes sure his kid hears his voice before the day is out.

Sources indicate that there’s a version of Ted Lasso in a different corner of the multiverse who gets swept up in the new job, the new city, the chaos of it all, and phones it in on the fatherhood front. This Ted doesn’t. He knows that presence isn’t always physical. Sometimes it’s a crackling FaceTime connection at midnight your time, 6 a.m. their time, just so your kid knows you’re still there.

It has been revealed that henry, during a video call, asks his dad if he’s ever run into The Beatles over there in England and whether he can get a photo with John, Paul, George, and Ringo. Now, Ted knows that both John Lennon and George Harrison have been dead for decades. He also knows his kid is 8 years old and asking with complete, genuine wonder. So Ted just agrees to try. He doesn't have the heart to kill that particular joy right now.

This one is subtle, but it matters. There's a real parenting skill in knowing when the truth can wait five minutes and when it needs to be delivered immediately. Ted isn't being dishonest — he's being developmentally attuned. There's a season for everything, as a certain king once sang from the stage of a Broadway house, and this particular season called for letting a little kid's imagination breathe. Ted will level with Henry about the hard stuff — and he does, plenty of times — but he picks his moments. That's wisdom.

When Michelle and Henry show up in London, Ted drops everything. They swing by the Crown and Anchor for an authentic English pub experience. They build a double-decker bus model at the kitchen table. And Henry settles into his happy place, sleeping between his parents. Even though Ted is in the midst of a brutal season, managing a locker room full of fragile egos while racking up losses, none of that matters for those few days. He is simply Dad.

What makes this moment rich is what we know that Henry doesn't: His parents' marriage is already over. Michelle is about to tell Ted she wants a divorce. And yet Ted keeps the joy intact for his son. He doesn't let his own grief occupy the visit. That is an act of real parenting discipline — the ability to compartmentalize your own pain long enough to give your child a memory that isn't shadowed by yours. Most of us have had to do some version of this. It doesn't feel heroic in the moment. It just feels hard. Ted does it anyway.

Henry asks Ted why, whenever he sees him on TV coaching soccer, he never seems to be doing anything. It's a kid's question, but it's actually a perfect question. Ted's answer is one of the most quietly profound things in the entire series. He tells Henry that once the game starts, he can't really tell his players what to do — he just has to hope that everything he's been trying to teach them made some kind of dent. Then he states: “It's kind of like being a father.”.

And then Henry, having absorbed none of this, is clearly already thinking about something else entirely. Ted realizes midsentence that his kid has mentally bounced. He stops talking. He smiles. He gets it. That moment is the whole job description of parenthood distilled into 30 seconds of television. You pour yourself into the role and hope it lands. You accept that you can't control the outcome. And you find a way to laugh about it — or at least smile — when your kid demonstrates, in real time, that they were not listening. Every parent reading this has lived this exact moment.

According to recent reports, henry isn’t the first kid to idolize a less-than-stellar role model, but his admiration for Jamie Tartt is a particular form of torture for Ted. As enigmatic as he is talented, Jamie makes Ted’s life incredibly difficult, even when he’s scoring goals. This puts Ted in a tough spot as Henry enthusiastically belts out the terribly annoying Baby Shark-themed Jamie Tartt song and sports his jersey with pride.

Sources indicate that but Ted lets his son revel in the moment of having access to the talented and popular starlet. He doesn’t even hint at the fact that perhaps Tartt isn’t the best guy to look up to. And when Jamie flashes Ted a smirk that makes his beautiful face even more punchable than usual while signing Henry’s jersey, Ted takes a deep breath and lets his son have a moment he’ll never forget.

Ted gets word from Michelle that Henry has been involved in a bullying situation at school — and then discovers it wasn't Henry who was bullied. Henry was the bully. Ted is shaken. And because of schedules and time zones, he has difficulty getting in touch with Henry right away.

If Ted had been around, he would likely have responded emotionally and sucked all the air out of the room. But when father and son finally get a chance to talk, Henry admits he messed up and didn't follow his dad's advice to count to 10 when he gets angry.

Sources indicate that with a little bit of forced space, Henry comes back around on his own. Ted doesn't strip his son of dignity while correcting him. And when Henry apologizes to his friend Doug with a rap in front of the class, you can almost hear Ted beaming through the phone. The lesson Ted had been repeating wasn't wasted — it just needed more time to work. Be a goldfish, sure, but also trust that the seeds you plant eventually grow. Even in the hardest soil.

Sources indicate that when Michelle and Henry leave London at the end of their visit, Ted walks them to the gate, knowing his marriage is essentially over and that his son doesn't know it. He says goodbye to Henry the way you say goodbye when you're not sure when you'll see each other again — fully present, holding it together, promising to talk soon. He watches Henry walk away with the airport attendant. And then the mask slips, just for a moment, and you see how much it costs him.

According to recent reports, here's what Ted doesn't do: He doesn't make the goodbye about himself. He doesn't get weepy in a way that burdens Henry with having to manage his father's emotions. He saves that for after the kid is out of sight. This is something parents don't talk about enough — the emotional labor of keeping your own grief off your child's plate. It's not suppression. It's protection. There's a version of this that's emotionally avoidant and unhealthy, but Ted's version in this moment is clear-eyed and loving. He feels everything. He just knows whose feelings need managing right now.

After Henry's visit to London ends and the lad heads back to Kansas, Ted does something small and wonderful. He reveals Henry, via video call, that he's placed the miniature Premier League Lego trophy Henry gave him into the Nelson Road Stadium Lego set they built together. It's a tiny thing. It's also everything.

Industry observers note that physical objects carry emotional weight for kids in ways that words sometimes can't. That Lego stadium becomes a shared artifact. It’s something Henry can picture when he thinks of his dad. Something that states “you were here, and you matter, and I kept a piece of what we made.”.

It's the parenting equivalent of keeping a drawing on the fridge forever. Henry even notices that Nate's Lego figure is at the back of the bench and asks about it, which gives Ted a gentle opening to explain that relationships can change without anyone being erased. Heavy stuff, delivered through the medium of tiny plastic soccer coaches.

Recent findings suggest that during their Lego video call conversation, Ted tells Henry that he doesn't love the idea of being away from him and that the only reason he's staying in England is that he's doing something key. Henry — who is, let's remember, about 10 years old — tells his dad to try to win the whole thing. Ted pushes back, saying winning isn't everything. And Henry indicates, essentially: “OK, but at least try.”.

It has been revealed that that's the moment a kid flips the script on you, and you realize they've been absorbing your lessons all along and also developing their own perspective on top of them. Ted doesn't dismiss the advice. He doesn't say “thanks, buddy” in that patronizing way parents sometimes do. He actually sits with it. He lets Henry be right.

In a recent development, kids need to see their parents receive feedback and adjust — it's how they learn that it's a normal and healthy thing to do. Plus, Henry is objectively correct. You can care about more than winning and still bring your whole effort to the field. That's not a contradiction. That's maturity.

Ted walks away from AFC Richmond. He turns down the job. He gets on the plane. He comes home to Kansas and, within about 60 seconds, is coaching Henry's junior league team, running plays, completely in his element.

Sources indicate that but the real parenting lesson isn't just that Ted comes home. It's why he comes home. He doesn't do it because the job went badly or because England rejected him. He does it because he looked at his life clearly and made an honest accounting of what mattered most. He highlighted his son — showed Henry in the most concrete way possible — that he is the priority. Not in the abstract, inspirational-poster way. In the literal, I-quit-my-dream-job-in-London-to-be-at-your-soccer-games way.

In a recent development, and then in the finale's final image, when Henry misses a shot and gets frustrated, Ted calls him over. Henry claims the words Ted has been saying all series — be a goldfish — and they both smile.

In a recent development, the lesson came back home. Same as the dad.

18 Easy Bean Recipes For Dinner That Are Cheap & Nutritious

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1141 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scarymommy

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that for a couple bucks a bag?
  • According to recent reports, like most American families, we’ve had to get pretty strategic about our grocery budget over the past year as grocery prices have risen (and risen, and risen...).
  • In a recent development, stuffed peppers are such a flavorful dish that even if you’re a meat-eater, you’ll never miss it in this recipe from All The Healthy Things.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that for a couple bucks a bag? You can’t beat ‘em.

According to recent reports, like most American families, we’ve had to get pretty strategic about our grocery budget over the past year as grocery prices have risen (and risen, and risen...). Since when did a pound of 80/20 become a special little treat? We’ve been opting for ground chicken and ground turkey instead for a few years now. As grocery prices continue to go up, what are you turning to to keep your own food bills down? Maybe it’s rice or lentils, but don’t forget about the humble bean. Canned beans and especially dried bagged beans are affordable sources of protein and fiber, and with the right bean recipes for dinner, you can make them so incredibly delicious. Here’s how to load them up with flavor.

In a recent development, stuffed peppers are such a flavorful dish that even if you’re a meat-eater, you’ll never miss it in this recipe from All The Healthy Things. Don’t be intimidated by the long ingredient list — most of them are just seasonings you most likely have in your pantry already. These only take about 15 minutes of prep, then just pop them in the oven and go help with homework or baths ‘til they’re done.

According to recent reports, burrito bowls are easy, and they never disappoint. Princess Pinky Girls’ recipe clearly includes chicken, but honestly, if you sub in some really tasty refried beans or something, you won’t even miss it. We are big on burrito bowls in my house because they’re also great work lunches to prep ahead of time.

According to recent reports, chickpeas, aka garbanzo beans, are the filling base to this super flavorful Italian chickpea salad from Foodie Crush. With all the additions — red onion, bell pepper, garlic, pepperoncini, and more — this is a delicious dense bean salad that’ll just get better as the flavors meld together in the fridge all week long.

In a recent development, averie Cooks’ Mediterranean white bean salad looks exactly like what I mean when I say I want a little snack, but can’t find anything I actually want in the fridge (it’s because I’m looking for a restaurant-quality appetizer at all times). This recipe is a bit more involved, but the marinated white beans, crispy asparagus, and shallots served over whipped ricotta sound good enough to be worth the trouble.

If you’re trying to up your fiber intake, Damn Delicious’ spinach and white bean soup is the recipe for you. This delicious dish is ready in 30 minutes and would be so, so good with some Parmesan grated on top and a side of crusty bread.

Chili is a major crowd-pleaser, and it’s a cheap way to make a lot of food at once, especially if you’re subbing in beans for beef. All The Healthy Things’ recipe includes meat, but you can just leave it out. That stated, don’t skip the little dash of cocoa powder — it’s a game-changer.

According to recent reports, being able to make some simple but delicious bean sides yourself is a great way to save money, and fortunately, Simply LaKita’s Southern baked beans fit the bill. It takes about an hour, but you’ll have a big batch to pair with other proteins throughout the week.

According to recent reports, I’m not sure falafel can be improved upon, but it’s fun to find out. What Jew Wanna Eat’s black bean falafel can be ready in about 20 minutes and doesn’t require many ingredients to pull off. Topped with tomatoes, cucumbers, and tzatziki, this is an easy and filling meal you’ll return to again and again.

If you’re having a bummer of a week, a cheesy, saucy enchilada night is guaranteed to make you feel at least 1% better. This version from Averie Cooks is a fantastic way to get more veggies into you and your kids, because the sweet potatoes and corn inside will indeed be coated in cheesy deliciousness.

Need a light, yummy salad to eat with chips for lunch? Or something easy to throw into burrito bowls or wraps? All The Healthy Things’ black bean and corn salad is easy to customize with your favorite veggies and herbs, and you can eat it in so many ways.

It has been revealed that filling, cheap taco ideas, you say? Damn Delicious has you covered with these black bean and quinoa tacos. They’re simple, satisfying, and inexpensive — the kind of recipe I could see going platinum in my house, personally.

Foodie Crush’s cannellini beans are another flavorful side you can pair with salads, proteins, or put on toast if you’re into that sort of thing. Or if you’re a fan of brothy beans, you can just grab the pot and a major spoon and dive in.

Industry observers note that princess Pinky Girl is the best at quick, easy recipes that are a breeze to make and super satisfying to eat. This cowboy casserole is also a one-pan meal (love) — it’s sort of like a chili base topped with cornbread. While her recipe calls for ground beef, you could easily just sub in extra beans and veggies.

Haute & Healthy Living’s Italian soup is rich and creamy thanks to a little coconut milk, and incredibly rich in flavor (shout-out to sun-dried tomatoes). The whole thing takes about 15 minutes of prep, and then the slow cooker will handle the rest for you.

These black bean burgers from Barefoot in the Pines take 35 minutes start to finish (hello, weeknight dinner MVP) and only take two cans of black beans, an onion, and some seasonings to pull off. You can top them with classic burger fixings or go with salsa and guac, as pictured here.

Recent findings suggest that fried plantains make a regular bowl of beans and rice feel special all of a sudden. This bowl by Cadry’s Kitchen is an easy, affordable meal that gets you all your food groups in one sitting. Like, if you had a nutritionist, they’d be so proud of you.

Recent findings suggest that I love a side of restaurant-style refried beans, but I never think to make them at home. Haute & Healthy Living’s version will help you keep the sodium in check without sacrificing flavor. Eat these as a side, a dip, or load up some bean and cheese burritos.

Beans and rice is a complete meal, and a delicious one at that. This recipe from Biscuits & Burlap is a copycat of Popeye’s red beans and rice side, which, if you’re from the South, you know they’ve got some of the best around.

Which bean dishes will you fall back on to save a few bucks each week?

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hope, grief, happiness, burnout — this week’s confessions have it all.

It has been revealed that is that... dare we say it... hope in the air?! This week’s anonymous mom confessions came in like a tidal wave. Literally, we’ve never seen so many 🌊 emojis in our inbox. Because, yes, moms wanted to talk about the midterms. Hundreds of them! Hope, relief, crying in the kitchen, feeling like they can breathe for the first time in years... along with a few who weren’t celebrating at all. We couldn’t even print a fraction of it, so please know, if you submitted one, you were in extremely plentiful tech giant.

But what also really struck us was the sentiment underneath: So many moms feel like they’re living in the in-between.

That tracks for the midterm results, obviously. Will we actually see change once the upcoming class gets sworn in this January? Meanwhile, families are still struggling with inflation and high gas prices and just generally being tired of being broke. This sentiment also surfaced in confessions from moms at crossroads in their relationships, whether it’s the precipice of divorce or considering starting a spicy affair. Moms are feeling it across the board, really, from parenting (the tween years are hitting some of you hard) to health (perimenopause purgatory strikes again).

According to recent reports, one mom kind of hit the nail on the head: Her personal life and finances are pretty much in shambles, and also, for the first time in a long time, she feels joy. Both. At once. That’s where a lot of you seem to be right now.

So there’s hope, and there’s the other thing, and most weeks they’re just two wings on the same bird. If that sounds familiar, you’ll likely find a lot of validation in this week’s roundup.

Industry observers note that scary Mommy Confessions are a tried-and-true part of what makes our site so fun. If you want to anonymously confess, look for our weekly callouts on Instagram. And to browse past Confessions, take a look here.

The Awkward Truth About Gym Class

📅 15 Jul 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1488 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fatherly

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This was my earliest memory of physical education: our teacher, a tall and thin woman whose broad nimbus of dark hair was edged with gray, asking us to make-believe.
  • Not that I was craving, or ever did crave, a traditional gym class.
  • It has been revealed that at the same time, I was physical.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Pretend you’re a tree. This was my earliest memory of physical education: our teacher, a tall and thin woman whose broad nimbus of dark hair was edged with gray, asking us to make-believe. By, as I understood it, not moving. In gym class. I was in second grade, and I was already confused. Somewhere here in my elementary school’s wood-floored gymnasium, I knew, there were ropes to climb, mats to tumble on, balls to kick and throw and dodge. And yet we were being corralled into this dumbed-down modern dance — the kind of hippie sh*t, I would later understand, that was typical of our Western Massachusetts college town.

Not that I was craving, or ever did crave, a traditional gym class. I was not made for gym. I was small — perpetually the second shortest boy in my grade — and slight and uninterested in the major sports that make up the bulk of public-school gym. I did not own a catcher’s mitt; no sane, responsible adult would let this shrimp play football.

It has been revealed that at the same time, I was physical. I was a kid, after all. I wanted to run around, try a handstand, lift a dumbbell, shoot a basket, make a goal. And as uncoordinated and unenthusiastic as I was, I was not entirely untalented. I remember running a seven-minute mile in fourth grade. I could touch my toes and put one foot behind my head. My friend Jason and I competed to see who would be the first to knock out 60 sit-ups in a minute. I don’t remember who won.

The psychosexual torture continued when gym class turned, for one whole day, to ballroom dance class.

According to recent reports, those achievements and activities, however, had nothing to do with gym class as I experienced it. In the same way that English class was not designed to make philistines love literature, or biology to inspire dedication to the scientific method, gym class was not about converting us into athletes. Instead, it was a class for the kids who already were athletes, who played baseball and field hockey for fun, who owned weight machines at home, who didn’t need to sit through the gym teacher’s confounding explanation of what it meant to be “offsides.” I didn’t begrudge them their special class. I could spell and do algebra. They could throw an arcing spiral. This was the way of the world, even in a Massachusetts town full of ex-hippies.

And that all would have been just fine — if gym class had stuck with the most mainstream of sports. I could suck at soccer and blow at basketball, because who cared? Instead, gym class branched out, and in those more marginal activities, it became an hour of dread.

Swimming was a particular source of trauma. When I was 8, during a year my family spent living in Brighton, England, I was so tearfully reluctant to get in the pool that the headmaster of the school had to personally throw me in. And as I got older, the trauma morphed: Back in Massachusetts, the locker room after eighth-grade swimming lessons was a horror movie — I, the underdeveloped shrimp, had to undress surrounded by my Sasquatchian contemporaries. I have a memory of once changing entirely inside a locker, but that can’t be real. Those things were barely 10 inches wide. But another memory is definitely real: During one class, I dived into the deep end — and the force of the water as I entered yanked my swimsuit to my ankles. I don’t know how I had the wherewithal to pull them up before surfacing, but I did. I guess I was learning something.

Recent findings suggest that the psychosexual torture continued when gym class turned, for one whole day, to ballroom dance class. Already awkward around girls, not to mention the implied romance of ballroom dance, I had the misfortune to be paired with Turtle Butt. Who was Turtle Butt? I don’t know. She was a girl I’d never spoken to, but one of my good friends had decided to call her Turtle Butt, even though, as far as I could tell, her butt did not resemble a turtle. And I was going to have to dance with her! Oh, the humiliation!

Gym class has always branched out from mainstream sports — and in those more marginal activities, it became an hour of dread.

Sources indicate that nearly 40 years later, I can now acknowledge that the humiliation was solely in my own head. I remember the potential embarrassment with infinitely more clarity than I remember any actual jeers or taunts, because there were none. But such is the world of the adolescent, where fears and anxieties dwarf reality.

And what I feared most of all was being seen. In other classes this didn’t happen. You might know where the Mason-Dixon Line was — or not. You might know how to deploy the quadratic formula — or not. Either way, you were not exposing anything about yourself other than your intellectual ability, or lack thereof.

It was similar in gym class. We all knew that some kids had it and some didn’t, and there was no shame in being terrible. (Asthma reduced my mile time to 20 minutes by eighth grade. But so what?) The difference, however, was that in gym class, unlike in history or math, you were a physical being. Strip away your ability to perform, and there you still stood, surrounded by your classmates, in sneakers and sweats or the jeans and T-shirt you wore to school that morning. You could pretend you’re a tree all you want — you remained visible: your prepubescent stature, your hairless lack of muscle tone, your terrapin posterior. There were no desks to hide behind, no escape from their eyes and their judgment.

No escape — except, perhaps, to grow up a little. In high school, my family moved to Southeastern Virginia, a place you’d think would have a sports and gym-class culture more extreme than that of the academic Yankees. Instead, gym was even more of an afterthought, not even required after sophomore or maybe junior year. Just like in second grade, I was confused. The school was full of jocks — guys who played soccer and football, girls on the field hockey team — and yet gym class was lackadaisical at best. Driver’s ed occupied a couple of months of the curriculum, and on Fridays, we’d ride a school bus to a nearby bowling alley, where nerds like me, who had no hope of throwing a strike, could at least show off by knowing how to score the game correctly.

Like so much of school, gym class had little to do with real life beyond offering up a few superficial options that might, one day, many years later, be of interest. Or not.

Sources indicate that in fact, I considered the bowling alley my place — because I was there all the time, after school. Technically, not in the bowling alley, but just outside, where almost every day I would meet my skateboarder friends to ride the concrete drainage ditch next to its parking lot. In high school, skating had become my life, my all-consuming hobby, my… my… sport? Yes, my sport! After having failed at all of the mainstream sports, I’d finally found this one sweaty, filthy, wonderful way to be an athlete (though I would never have used that word back then). And while I wasn’t pro material, I wasn’t too bad at it, either. I could hold my own among my friends, at competitions in Virginia Beach, on road trips to Richmond and Washington, D.C. And more important, I could do so without fretting about being seen, in some unspeakable way, by the kids around me. Skateboarding required us to accept one another, in all our foibles and weirdnesses. Because if we didn’t, then who would we skate with?

I stuck with skateboarding for most of a decade, before aging out postcollege and taking up distance running and, more recently, rock climbing. As with skateboarding, I’m pretty good at both, if not truly exceptional, and I appreciate the physical experience of each in ways I could not have imagined in high school. At times, I’ve wondered: If gym class had taught us how to run, or how to scale a boulder, would I have discovered and loved those sports decades earlier? Somehow, I doubt it. Like so much of school, gym class had little to do with real life beyond offering up a few superficial options that might, one day, many years later, be of interest. Or not. What mattered was what happened after school, in every sense of the term. Still, gym class did teach me this one vital lesson about public education: If you make like a tree, you can leave.

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1187 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scarymommy

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I don’t care if I’m reliant on it and you can’t make me.
  • Sleep deprivation is a form of torture.
  • As a kid, I remember lying in bed for long stretches of time before I could fall asleep.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I don’t care if I’m reliant on it and you can’t make me.

Sleep deprivation is a form of torture. At some point in every adult’s life, you find out why the hard way. Every parent goes through intense sleep deprivation when they bring home their first baby, and every subsequent newborn after that. But for some of us, sleep never came easy. By the time the babies came on the scene, we were well acquainted with the wee hours of the morning, what it felt like to be up all night, every night.

As a kid, I remember lying in bed for long stretches of time before I could fall asleep. My thoughts would race about everything and nothing. I had a dream catcher above my bed to ward off nightmares, worry dolls under my pillow to whisper my anxieties to so they could “hold them for me” until the morning, and my bedroom TV volume on low while a plucky Disney Channel show played. At sleepovers I was always the last to fall asleep, if I managed to stay overnight at all.

Industry observers note that I didn’t get a formal anxiety diagnosis until I went off to college many years later, but learning more about my brain finally gave me an understanding of why sleep was so elusive. With a nervous system stuck in fight-or-flight mode, of course I’d wake at the slightest sound and have a nearly impossible time winding down enough to knock out at the end of the day.

According to recent reports, finally, in 2019, I expressed my frustrations to my fresh psychiatrist. I was awake for hours every night waiting for sleep to come, while my husband was already in REM before he ever got fully horizontal on the mattress. I tried guided meditations (why do all the beach ones feature squawking seagulls?) and binaural beats and exercising with the goal of exhausting myself during the day, but my insomnia had reached a frustrating new intensity. It was making my anxiety and depression so much worse; I looked and felt utterly bedraggled. So, he prescribed me trazodone.

While trazodone isn’t a true sedative — it’s actually an antidepressant — it’s often used off-label to treat insomnia because it gives you a similar relaxing, drowsy feeling. My doctor told me that it’s not a controlled substance and carries a very low risk of addiction, but that mentally, I might start to feel like I need it in order to sleep. If I didn’t like feeling dependent on it, we could make some changes.

“Are they going to stop making it any time soon?” I asked.

“Is it bad to take long-term for any other reason?”.

“Then I’m perfectly fine with being mentally addicted,” I remarked. And I’ve taken it every single night since then.

Recent findings suggest that research has shown again and again that regularly sleeping well is a key quality-of-life indicator. Lack of sleep negatively impacts every system of the body, weakening the immune system, worsening mental health, and increasing risk of countless conditions, from high cholesterol to Alzheimer’s. Women are twice as likely to have insomnia as men, which has been attributed to our natural hormonal fluctuations throughout the month and the fact that we tend to carry the lion’s share of the mental load in the family, on top of being more prone to mood disorders.

It has been revealed that yet even though we know all of this, taking anything to help you fall asleep is still... kind of frowned upon. Researchers in the UK conducted focus groups interviewing people who take prescription sleep medications and OTC supplements, like melatonin, and found that they had a lot of internalized stigma around the subject — even when talking about it in a room full of people who also take something to help them sleep.

Recent findings suggest that they found that participants were very deliberate in how they explained their need for their meds. They’re deserving (explaining that their condition, like chronic pain or anxiety, makes sleep impossible without medication). They’re compliant, only ever taking their meds exactly as prescribed (or, in the case of supplements, as directed on the label). They’re responsible, always watching themselves for signs of addiction or misuse. They expressed extreme guilt over taking more of their medications than they should, or trying alternative medications meant to make them sleepy when their usual prescription wasn’t enough.

We recently asked Scary Mommy’s Instagram followers the question, “Do you take anything to fall asleep at night?” Some of that same stigma highlighted up in their responses too.

Multiple readers said they take Gravol when they can’t sleep, calling it a “horrid habit” or something they only do “when things get really bad.” Another said, “I can’t sleep without a quarter of an Ambien. It’s terrible!” “Haven’t had an unmedicated sleep in 7+ years 🫠,” said one response. The melting face is doing a lot of heavy lifting there.

Recent findings suggest that of course there were plenty of Scary Mommies who felt no shame (that’s sort of our shtick around here). In response to the question “Do you take anything to fall asleep?” one user simply replied, “WINE.” Plenty of other respondents also take trazodone, or Unisom, or some other sleep aid. Weed, whether in vape or gummy form, is also an extremely popular option. See also: a large number of replies indicating they take magnesium and progesterone at night thanks to perimenopause, and that HRT was finally the thing to help them sleep through the night.

But one response really captures my feelings about the whole subject:.

According to recent reports, “Oh lord I’m so medicated. But it’s working.”.

Even on the days I feel like I shouldn’t have to take something to help me sleep, that perhaps I could sleepmaxx or wellness hack my way out of having to take a pill every night, I remind myself that not getting enough sleep is literally deadly.

When you’re someone who struggles with sleep night after night, you know how rapidly your mental and physical health can plummet. Insomnia decimates my quality of life. Sleep deprivation locks my personality and my joy away behind a concrete wall where I can’t access them anymore. It impacts my longevity and my relationships. While I’m not saying every reader who responded has a healthy way of getting to sleep at night, or that we shouldn’t be critical of our relationships with substances, I think we could all use a little validation that not getting enough sleep is, in fact, torturous.

More moms need to hear that they deserve to sleep well. They should know that their doctors want to hear from them if they feel abnormally tired during the day. And I want more women to internalize the idea that this world is hard enough to live in as it is. You should at least be able to meet it each day not feeling like a shell of yourself.

And that’s why you can pry my trazodone out of my cold, dead hands.

Tech Report: 10 Great Sports Docs & True-Life Stories To Stream With Your Kids Right Now

📅 15 Jul 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1171 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fatherly

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • From inspiring stories to crucial moments in history to cutting edge contermporary atheletes, there’s a great co-viewing experience for everyone.
  • Sources indicate that finding movies and TV that please everyone can be tough.
  • Industry observers note that sports docuseries, or true-to-life dramatized sports stories, are great to watch with young athletes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

From inspiring stories to crucial moments in history to cutting edge contermporary atheletes, there’s a great co-viewing experience for everyone.

Sources indicate that finding movies and TV that please everyone can be tough. But if you’ve got a sporty kid, screen time is a great opportunity. Sure, there’s old-school sports movie like The Sandlot or A League of Their Own — complete with inspirational messages and strong moral codes. But why go for fictional sports stories when you can get the real thing?

Industry observers note that sports docuseries, or true-to-life dramatized sports stories, are great to watch with young athletes. They tell inspirational tales and maybe even give them a real-life role model in the meantime. From a variety of different sports to a selection of different formats, we’ve thought about the watchability and the relevance of each of these selections. There should be something for everyone in this list. And, at the very least, with each, you and your kid will learn something.

In a recent development, this documentary film focuses on several different Paralympic athletes, all of whom have truly amazing stories. Warning for parents: This documentary is not for the faint of heart, as some of the physical challenges are truly harrowing. For example, Bebe Vio — who inspired the name of the documentary — lost all of her limbs to meningitis at the age of 11. She nonetheless went on to become a wheelchair fencer. Deeply inspiring, this doc is great for teens interested in sports and perhaps great for all of us to have a little perspective on the amazing nature of the human spirit.

According to recent reports, the 2004 story of the Boston Red Sox is a great one in terms of an underdog story. Even if you’re not a Red Sox fan, this story represents a very specific time in baseball and tells the story of how this iconic team broke a curse that had existed since 1918. If your kid is just starting to get into baseball, this documentary series might seem like ancient history; after all, 2004 was more than 20 years ago. And yet, this particular season for many of us feels very recent and still relevant.

It has been revealed that who doesn’t love trick shots? This 30 for 30 ESPN doc is all about a group of five guys who were former college roommates who created a sports comedy entertainment phenomenon. Focused on trick shots and betting, this doc is 100% for older kids. But if you’ve got a teen who is into sports and loves to joke around, this is a great, quirky documentary focused on male friendship, humor, and creating something nobody has ever done before.

Recent findings suggest that everybody is obsessed with Travis Kelce, but his brother Jason Kelce might be the more interesting of the siblings, at least as an athlete. The 2023 documentary film chronicles the 2022 Philadelphia Eagles season, with a specific focus on Kelce. The main tension here is whether or not Kelce will retire from the NFL. Weird topic for kids? Well, for tweens and teens interested in unpacking the real-deal toll of being in the NFL, there’s something smartly educational about this. You may be young and obsessed with football now, but life is long.

Not technically a documentary, this is a docudrama based on the true story of Ray McElrathbey, who deals with a ton of family adversity and racism. Set in the early 2000s, McElrathbey’s story is inspiring and very family-oriented. Again, this one might be for older kids, but the script is from Nick Santora of Reacher and Sopranos fame, so there’s a breezy and very focused feeling to this movie.

According to recent reports, here’s another docudrama that is based on a real-life movement in India, centered on teenagers and skateboarding culture. In the film, a young girl named Prerna (Rachel Sanchita Gupta) finds purpose and belonging through skateboarding. The film is a heartwarming coming-of-age movie, but watching it with your kid means you’re also giving them a dose of contemporary history. The production for the film also worked very closely with rural villages in India to make sure it accurately portrayed the culture and struggles of teenagers.

A great one to watch with your aspiring skateboarding kid, or maybe a kid who isn’t sure what their athletic interest might be.

In a recent development, one of the greatest athletes of our time is also the subject of a one-of-a-kind docuseries. Released in 2024, Simone Biles Rising is all about the gymnast’s comeback. The fact that Biles has been so transparent about her mental health has been a groundbreaking part of the conversations about young athletes. As both a role model and someone who is part of living history, Biles is a figure that should inspire conversation with your curious athlete.

This 10-part documentary changed everything back in 2020. However, at this point, The Last Dance — which tells the story of one of the greatest periods of the Chicago Bulls — almost feels vintage. Chances are, for certain parents, you didn’t have a kid old enough to watch this documentary nearly seven years ago. And, if you’re of the generation that lived through the Bulls’ 1990s dynasty, then you owe it to share that history with your kid.

Not everything about Michael Jordan and his teammates is admirable, to be clear. But the thing about some great sports history is that it can be messy.

Focused on the 2024 X Games, The Rise: Gold Medal Girls of the X Games focuses on four teen athletes, Arisa Trew, Shiloh Catori, Reese Nelson, and Jada Ward. Those are all skateboarders, and that’s just the most recent season. More broadly, The Rise covers all sorts of women’s sports, from skating to the WNBA. If you have a young woman looking for some latest role models, you can’t miss with the various seasons of The Rise.

Sources indicate that you can really start anywhere with this excellent docuseries. But the most recent season of Tour de France: Unchained is focused on the 2024 Tour de France. Obviously, the famous bicycle race has existed since 1903, but it’s really only recently that we could actually document this incredible event. Even the least sporty kid in the world can get excited about people using their bodies to propel a bicycle forward. And the most sporty kids will have trouble wrapping their mind around the sheer effort it takes to traverse 2,200 miles over 24 days over some of the hilliest terrain on Earth.

The most recent season of Tour de France: Unchained, released in 2025, is now the last season of this docuseries. The real Tour de France hasn’t gone anywhere, of course. In fact, it’s happening right now. Meaning if you get your kid excited enough, you can watch the 2026 Tour de France as it’s happening. Or watch a little contemporary Tour de France, then go back and watch Unchained on Netflix.

Tech Report: 29 Gifts For Moms Whose Favorite Form Of Therapy Is Travel

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Here are some of our favorite travel-forward finds.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

You can never go wrong with travel gifts, TBH.

Sources indicate that jSome clichés are clichés for a reason. Being a mom is really hard. But it’s so, so rewarding. Also, travel is the best teacher. For many moms, those three clichés are often true in tandem. Sometimes, the lessons we learn during travel make the invisible load of motherhood a little lighter to bear. Sometimes, the lesson is simply that we have to make time for ourselves to be the best moms we can be. And sometimes, seeing the world through our kids’ eyes is enough to remind us that even when the road is rough, the reward is usually worth it.

Industry observers note that so, when it comes to gifts you can give the moms in your life, it’s hard to beat travel gifts... especially when travel already seems to be their favorite form of therapy. While splurging on things as pricey as plane tickets or an all-inclusive resort stay is (understandably) out of reach for many of us, there are tons of items any travel-loving mom would be overjoyed to get. We should know! The Scary Mommy editors are all busy moms who enjoy squeezing getaways and adventures into whatever little pockets of spare time we can find.

Here are some of our favorite travel-forward finds.

I have the full-size Naturepedic pillow, and I yearn to own the travel-sized one too. I have chronic neck pain and headaches, so I need a soft yet supportive pillow and one that is comfortable when sleeping on my back or my side. I’ve purchased and used so many pillows in my day, and this is finally THE ONE. I love that you can customize how much stuffing you keep inside, and I like to form mine with a little divot for my head to maximize my neck support. The full-size is heavy, though, so I really want to find a travel-sized one under the tree this year to use instead of the down (deeply unsupportive) hotel pillows that leave me hurting. — Katie McPherson, Associate Editor, Lifestyle & Entertainment.

This is the diaper bag I wish I’d had for every family trip with little ones! It fits a pump, bottles, diapers, a laptop... really, you’d be surprised how much stuff you can stuff in it. I especially love that there’s a quick-grab pocket on the front sized perfectly for wipes. Even though my kids are teens, I carry this as a carry-on backpack because it’s so pretty and functional, and it slips right over your suitcase handle so you have one less thing to juggle at the gate. Thanks to the easy-clean neoprene and chic design, it doesn’t scream “diaper bag.” — Julie Sprankles, Deputy Editor, Lifestyle & Entertainment.

In a recent development, the Cincha Go-Tote has become my most-reached-for travel bag because it solves the one problem every traveler has: The carry-on that tips over every time you let go of it. The Cincha Go-Tote has a built-in luggage sleeve that slides right over your suitcase handle so everything stays put, and your hands stay free; plus it is water-resistant, has leather accents that make it look way more elevated than a travel bag has any right to look, and fits everything you need for a flight without becoming a black hole. This is for the traveler on your holiday list who has everything but still somehow does not have this. — Katie Garrity, Senior Editor, News & Social.

Sources indicate that I have bought my fair share of travel pillows over the years, and a lot of them just... don't get the job done. I love this one because it stuffs into a small sack and it really does help you nod off on the plane without choking or smothering you. When I travel with this, people always ask me where it's from. — Sarah Aswell, Deputy Editor, News & Social.

I think my newly introduced favorite obsession is traveling with a trunk! For those trips when you need the extra space, this beauty lets you travel in style. It has such a sophisticated vintage-inspired look... it feels like it should be loaded onto the Orient Express. That old-world glamour even extends to a sleek double-latch closure (instead of a zipper) with TSA-approved locks. She’s not just pretty, though; she’s durable too, thanks to a tough polycarbonate shell, reinforced corners, and replaceable wheels. And once you get used to traveling trunk-style with its super-convenient deep side, it’ll be hard to go back! — Julie Sprankles.

Packing for a trip with kids usually means digging through a black hole for one sock, and these clear, color-coded organizers fix that. The set of four comes in substantial, medium, and mini sizes with windows so you can see exactly what’s inside, and my favorite part is that each one gets its own job, like clothes, snacks, or tech and first aid. They’re the unglamorous travel upgrade that makes packing and unpacking take minutes instead of hours, and I’m never traveling without them again!— Katie Garrity.

Sources indicate that I don't know how many times I've had a fully charged battery back with me while traveling, but I can't find the right cord to attach it to my phone. This magnetic charger is small, mighty, and charges cordlessly! It has become my number one charging brick, and that notes a lot coming from me. This is one of those products where you buy one and then almost immediately buy another one, just to have a spare. I also love getting these as gifts for people! — Sarah Aswell.

My non-negotiable for travel days is comfort, but I don’t want to look like I rolled right out of bed and onto the plane, either. These Cozy Earth joggers are just the ticket. They’re ridiculously soft, with a slim-but-relaxed fit and an adjustable drawstring that’s perfect for long flights. And the burgundy color is seriously stunning, so I look put-together even though I feel like I’m in my comfiest PJs. — Julie Sprankles.

Ask anyone who knows me, and they'll tell you my happy place is sitting out in the sun — wherever that may be. As someone who has long loved Gray Malin's art (but not someone who has been able to splurge on it as often as I'd like), these travel pouches make a great happy medium. I love how packable and useful these travel pouches are, but what I love most about them is how "in the mood" they'll get you to travel. As you pack up your stuff, you can practically taste vacation. What's not to love? — Kate Auletta, Editor in Chief.

For the traveler on your list who is still hauling around a beat-up suitcase, this is the upgrade that will make them feel like a seasoned jet-setter, with a slim aluminum frame and polycarbonate shell that look as sleek as they are tough. The 77-liter interior has a built-in compression panel for squeezing in just a little more and about 1.5 inches of extra depth, which is exactly what you need for a 7- to 10-day trip. It also has 360° spinner wheels and two TSA-approved locks, so it’s the gift that makes every airport trip a little less stressful! — Katie Garrity.

In a recent development, like many people entering their 40s after a lifetime of wear and tear, I deal with a lot of foot issues, especially when I'm walking 20,000 steps a day while traveling. I love these shoe inserts that have gotten me through the most epic travel days, including 12-mile days at Disney World and a 15-mile day hike in Glacier National Park. — Sarah Aswell.

While experts generally agree that airlines don’t reuse blankets, it’s still comforting just to carry your own on board. As someone who is always cold, I can’t tell you how much I appreciate being able to toss this into my carry-on. It comes with a super-soft throw, a matching eye mask, and the coordinating bag to stash them both in. — Julie Sprankles.

Industry observers note that this is the carry-on to match all carry-ons! This backpack opens super wide at the top so you can find anything you need, plus it has a large front zippered pocket for chargers, snacks, or notes from admirers. It fits so much stuff and yet still somehow slides perfectly under an airplane seat like some kind of backpack sorcery. — Katie Garrity.

It’s just designed to fit so much more, even though it takes up the same amount of space as other bags. Used with the packing cubes from the same organization, I can easily fit a week’s worth of stuff into a bag and not have to check anything. — Sarah Aswell.

Marshall is such an iconic brand that I feel a little cooler every time I slip these headphones on. There are lots of reasons they’re great for tossing in your carry-on. The adaptive noise cancellation automatically blocks out plane noises, but one push of a button switches to transparency mode so I can hear flight announcements. The battery lasts up to 50-plus hours with ANC on. And, one of my favorite features, they’re made to fold up small so you can stash them in your bag without a hassle. — Julie Sprankles.

This tote organizer turns any bottomless pit of a bag into an orderly dream. With pockets and pouches for all of your on-the-go essentials, the ToteSavvy makes traveling a breeze. — Katie Garrity.

It has been revealed that S'well makes my favorite lunch salad bowl container; it never leaks and is super high-quality. So when I saw that the same firm came out with a travel bottle set, I knew that I wanted it! All of their products are so well-designed and thoughtful; these bottles are made of lightweight material, and they haven't leaked yet. They also come in a super cute lightweight pouch. — Sarah Aswell.

In a recent development, my husband travels for work, so he flies multiple times per week. He’s been using the Airback MAX for about a year now, and it has held up remarkably well to his strenuous schedule! But what he really loves is that it lets him skip checking a bag because it has a built-in vacuum system that sucks air out of your clothes. That means you can fit 25+ items in this one carry-on-sized bag. It also converts from a rolling trolley to a backpack in seconds, has dual TSA-approved locks, USB ports, and an expandable compression bag that doubles as a laundry bag. — Julie Sprankles.

Recent findings suggest that the scariest part of any flight is wondering how long the entertainment is going to last, and this kit is built to keep toddlers 18 months and up busy from takeoff to landing without a single screen. It comes with a first-flight storybook that helps set expectations before you board, which is a small thing that makes a big difference when a little one has never been on a plane. It’s compact, screen-free, and designed by Lovevery’s play experts, so it’s one more thing I don’t have to worry about in the carry-on. — Katie Garrity.

For a bag that barely weighs a pound when unpacked and tucks away neatly into a small zippered square, you’ll be shocked by how much The Foldie actually holds: When fully expanded, it has a 40-liter packing volume. The expandable bottom adds just the right amount of extra space when needed. We love that it’s a great size to use as your carry-on or to tuck into your suitcase for bringing home souvenirs. I’ve been using this bag heavily for almost two years now, and it’s still one of my absolute favorites. Not only does it still look great, but I get asked about it all the time! — Julie Sprankles.

In a recent development, I fully admit I got one of these after seeing a social media video of a before-and-after. This thing really does depuff your face... and if you're like me, my face can get pretty puffy while traveling. Carrying this with me and having it after I get off the plane or after a long car ride just makes me feel better. And even besides the de-puffing benefits, it feels really good, too. — Sarah Aswell.

I love that the Woda is the brainchild of two moms living in Charleston, South Carolina, who needed something hands-free that could be hosed down after days on the coast with their kids. For moms who love to pack up the car and head to the nearest beach as much as possible, you can’t get a better gift than this super-durable yet lightweight waterproof backpack. Made from a non-toxic EVA foam, it’s mold- and mildew-resistant, meaning she won’t have to worry about it getting funky after a day on the water. And it’s seriously roomy with a carrying capacity of up to 30 pounds! — Julie Sprankles.

Industry observers note that any traveler knows long flights cause blood flow in the legs to slow down since you’re seated for extended periods. That, in turn, can increase the risk of health issues like deep vein thrombosis. Compression socks are a simple way to help blood vessels work more efficiently on long flights, reducing the risk of swelling and blood clots. Trust us when we say that Dr. Motion compression socks are out here compressioning! And they come in so many cute patterns, which is so girly to say... but we don’t care. — Katie Garrity.

In a recent development, what did I do before packing cubes? I love these by JanSport because they are larger than most and fit perfectly in my suitcase side by side. The smaller "cube" is great for carrying an extra pair of undies and a spare shirt in my carry-on. They also have a see-through mesh front and a carrying handle, which make a huge difference. And never forget that JanSport items all come with an incredibly wonderful lifetime warranty. — Sarah Aswell.

I’m a carry-on girlie whenever I can be, but some trips just require more space. And if I’m going to be checking a bag, I want it to fit everything without being too cumbersome. This Monos Medium Check-in is the perfect size because it’s roomy without being obnoxiously major. Plus, the limited-edition Mulberry color is a deep, glossy purple that is beyond dreamy! Add in the fact that it’s durable, has a TSA-accepted lock, and super-glidable wheels, and I genuinely get excited at the mere thought of packing for my next trip. — Julie Sprankles.

It’s a toss-up when it comes to what’s more vexing: using generic hotel bar soap to wash your face or having to buy fresh face wash when you get where you’re going because you can’t carry on your fave. That’s why I’m a substantial fan of Olay Cleansing Melts. These portable cleansing squares are TSA-friendly since they’re water-activated, so you can toss ‘em in your purse or carry-on. — Kate Auletta.

It has been revealed that raise your hand if you’ve ever frantically patted down every pocket in an airport security line, convinced you lost your passport (me, it’s definitely me). So when I needed a fresh passport holder, I knew I wanted one with a bit of built-in peace of mind. This Spotminders Passport Holder Air works with Apple’s Find My app, meaning I can see exactly where my passport is in about two seconds. It’s ultra-slim but still has room for my license and a few other cards, plus a dedicated flap for boarding passes. Right now there’s a buy-two-get-one-free deal, which makes it a smart pick if you’re looking to upgrade the whole family before a major trip. — Julie Sprankles.

It’s the one piece of luggage that makes a two-week family trip feel organized instead of chaotic! — Katie Garrity.

For trips when I don’t have room for over-ear headphones, these Nothing Ear (3a) earbuds pack a ton of travel-ready power into a punchy, pocket-sized case. #160520. Get Into a Back-to-School Mindset With Advice From 12 Youth Soccer Coaches

📅 16 Jul 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2112 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fatherly ↗ Open Full Page

Get Into a Back-to-School Mindset With Advice From 12 Youth Soccer Coaches

📅 16 Jul 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2112 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fatherly

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Start the school year off on the right foot with insights from coaches who understand how the game translates to life off the field.
  • According to recent reports, late summer is always the hardest on parents.
  • The back-to-school transition is never the clean handoff the calendar makes it look like.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Start the school year off on the right foot with insights from coaches who understand how the game translates to life off the field.

According to recent reports, late summer is always the hardest on parents. The pool days are numbered. The long evenings are shortening. The school year is coming, and it doesn’t care how ready you are.

The back-to-school transition is never the clean handoff the calendar makes it look like. Every August, we tell ourselves this year will be different. You’ll get ahead of it. Lunch prep sorted by Sunday. Bedtime routine locked in a week early. Screen-time rules clearly communicated and actually enforced. You’ll draw up this plan with the kind of granular, paranoid attention to detail that Guardiola brings to a cup final. But then, it’s all a disaster by Tuesday.

If you’re looking for an actual strategy that holds up, go to the park on a Saturday morning, find the sideline, and start listening to whoever is coaching.

These are people managing every extreme of human emotion — low blood sugar, wounded pride, full-on existential crises — all while trying to stop a five-way argument over who gets the neon green goalie pinnies. If they don’t know something useful, nobody does. So we hit up a dozen youth soccer coaches for their best back-to-school advice.

I tell my girls this on the first day of every season, and I mean it every time. Some days we’re doing your favorite thing. Some days we’re doing the thing you hate. The thing you hate is usually the thing that needs work. That’s not a coincidence. I don’t let them skip the hard drills because they don’t feel like it. I don’t let them drift to the stuff they’re already good at and call it practice. That’s not practice. That’s just playing around.

Industry observers note that the subject your kid is dreading going back to — that’s the one. That’s the drill they need to run. Don’t negotiate them out of it. Make the deal: Do the work first, then we talk. It’s the same conversation I have at practice every Tuesday and Thursday, and it works there, too.

Industry observers note that I don’t do big speeches. I never have. I’ve seen coaches do the whole thing — the whiteboard, the clipboard, the fire-and-brimstone season opener — and the kids are bored by the second sentence. So I just ask one question: What kind of teammate do you want? And they tell me. Funny. Helpful. Somebody who doesn’t make you feel bad when you mess up. Somebody who actually passes the ball. I write it all down. Then I say, good — now be all of that.

Sources indicate that it’s not complicated. It’s just that nobody asks them the question directly and then holds them to the answer. Try it before school starts. Ask your kid what kind of friend they want to have this year. Then have the second half of that conversation.

I’ve been doing this since before most of these parents were driving their kids to practice, and the one thing that has never changed is this: Effort is the one thing every single kid controls completely. Talent, you’re born with, or you’re not. Height, same thing. But running back on defense when you’re tired? Picking yourself up after a bad touch and going again? That’s a choice. I’ve had kids with every physical tool in the world coast through and wonder why they weren’t improving. I’ve had kids who couldn’t trap a ball if their life depended on it go on to be captains because they simply refused to stop working.

Industry observers note that teachers see it the same way I do. The kid who stays after, asks questions, turns things in on time — that kid builds a reputation. And that reputation opens doors that talent alone doesn’t.

Every season, I get at least one kid who shows up on day one with opinions. Wants to play a different position, run a different shape, do things the way her last team did it. And look — I love that. I want players who think about the game. But there’s an order of operations. You don’t get to redesign a system you don’t understand yet. So the rule is: First month, you learn why we do what we do. Why we press from the front. Why we switch the point of attack the way we do.

Once you understand the why, then you’ve earned the right to push back.

A fresh school year means new teachers with their own ways of doing things. The kid who spends the first few weeks actually paying attention — figuring out how this classroom works before deciding what they think of it — that kid is so far ahead of the one who comes in with their arms already crossed.

Sources indicate that I have a rule on this team, and it has been the same rule since my first season: You get three seconds after a mistake. Three seconds to be upset, to be frustrated, to feel whatever you feel. Then your head comes back up, and you get back in position. Because here’s the thing: The play is still happening. The game didn’t stop because you had a bad touch. And if you’re standing there feeling sorry for yourself, you’re now two mistakes deep instead of one.

I tell parents this, too, because it applies to everything. Your kid is going to fail a test this year. They’re going to say something wrong in class and feel embarrassed about it. They’re going to have a bad day. In life situations off the field, you get more than three seconds, but the same lesson applies. Acknowledge the mistake and then head up, back in position. The recovery is the name of the game.

Sources indicate that I am obsessive about communication on the field. Obsessive. Not yelling, not blaming — information. Constant, useful, real-time information between players. Where you are, what you see, what they should do next. Most kids go completely silent under pressure, and that is exactly backwards from what you need. When it’s hardest to talk is when talking matters most.

I tell my players: A quiet team is a confused team. And a confused team gives the ball away. It’s the same thing off the field. The kid who speaks up in class, who claims hi to the kid sitting alone at lunch, who tells a friend when something’s wrong — that kid ends up in the middle of things. The good things. Make some noise this year. Say something.

In a recent development, I played college soccer, and I will tell you that the thing nobody taught me until it was almost too late was how to rest. We were all conditioned to think that more was always better — more sprints, more film, more time in the gym. And there’s a point where more just breaks you. The best thing I ever did for my game was learn to take recovery seriously. Sleep. Real sleep. Not optional, not a treat — part of the program.

Sources indicate that I build rest into my players’ weeks now, and I don’t let them feel guilty about it. The brain works the same way the body does. It consolidates everything it learned while you sleep. So if your kid is heading back to school and you’re letting them stay up until midnight on their phone — that’s not a small thing. That’s undermining everything they did that day. Rest is not laziness. I promise you it’s not.

It has been revealed that I’ve been watching kids show up to this field for a long time, and I can tell you — the ones who get there early are different. Not because they’re more talented. Because they’ve had time to settle in. They’ve already touched a ball, already talked to a teammate, already figured out where they are and what they’re doing before anything’s officially started. They’re comfortable. The ones sprinting in right at the whistle are always the ones who take the whole first half to find their rhythm.

In a recent development, so on the first day of school, get there early. Your kid will have the chance to find the right classroom, ask any questions, and breathe a little bit. It’s a small thing that changes the whole morning.

Recent findings suggest that I coach little kids. Eight-year-olds. So I see a lot of feelings on this field, and I’ve been real clear about my policy since day one: All the feelings are allowed. You can cry. You can tell me you need a minute. You can be upset. None of that is a problem. What you cannot do is walk off this field and decide you’re done. That’s the one thing I won’t accept. And I don’t say it mean — I just say it clearly, and I say it early, so it’s already been said when the moment comes.

Back to school is hard for a lot of kids, and I think parents sometimes feel like they’re supposed to pretend it isn’t. The anxiety is real. The overwhelm is real. Your kid can feel all of it and still go. That’s actually the lesson — that you’re allowed to struggle and still show up. Those two things can both be true at the same time.

I think about the game the way I think about conversation. There are moments when you have to speak — when you see the opening, and you have to take it, because if you wait, it’ll be gone. And there are moments when the best thing you can do is find the person in a better position and give it to them. The hardest thing to coach is the judgment between those two moments. A player who always shoots is a ball hog. A player who always passes is invisible. The great ones — the really great ones — know the difference in real time.

Recent findings suggest that that’s an ego conversation as much as it’s a soccer conversation. Knowing when to speak up in class and when to let someone else take the floor. When to lead a group project and when to step back and support. It’s one of the harder things to teach, and one of the more key ones. Start having that conversation now, before the year starts.

I want my players to come to me. That’s the whole thing. I make myself as available as I possibly can because I know from experience that the kids who ask questions are the ones who get better. Not always the most talented kids — just the ones who seek feedback and then actually do something with it. Every season, the gap I notice most isn’t about skill. It’s about which kids advocate for themselves and which ones wait to be noticed.

In a recent development, teachers work the same way I do. They want to help — they really do — but they’re managing a roomful of kids, and they can’t chase all of them down. The ones who stay after, send the email, ask what they missed and what they can do better — those are the ones who get more of the good stuff. It’s not about being the favorite. It’s about knowing how to ask for help. That skill will serve your kid for the rest of their life.

I coach at the level where it starts to get serious. Parents are thinking about high school rosters, kids are thinking about highlight reels, everybody’s tracking individual stats. And I am here to tell you — from where I stand on this sideline — that the players who make the biggest difference are almost never the ones you’d expect.

I’ve had physically gifted kids who played every game like it was an audition and made everyone around them worse for it. And I’ve had kids who, by every measurable standard, were average, who won us games because they made their teammates better. They covered for people, they communicated, and they did the stuff that doesn’t show up in the box score.

It has been revealed that we spend so much time on our kids as individuals — their grades, their performance, their future — that we sometimes forget to teach them how to be good at being part of something. That’s a skill too. Maybe the most crucial one. The school year is long and almost entirely a team sport. Remind them.

The list is built from a full year of Search trends across every category from tech to style. And this year, the toys and games section looks suspiciously like the inside of an elder millennial’s childhood toy chest.

Here are the trending toys parents will want to know about, plus what the list says about how we’re shopping this year.

Sources indicate that searches for “classic toy train set” climbed 240% this year, one of the biggest jumps Google shared. Wooden trains survive toddler teeth, being thrown down the stairs and never fail to get passed down more than once. (Expect the figure-eight to claim your living room floor for the next few years.).

Industry observers note that “A ton of play,” Google wrote, and we respect the pun. Searches for stuffed elephant plushies rose 240%, with the Pets Alive Baby Elephant Surprise as the featured pick. Plush is a good pick for a 1-year-old and a 10-year-old alike, and the right one becomes a friend for life.

Searches for the Fujifilm instax holiday set jumped 190%. For tweens, a camera that spits out a real photo is a nice break from the phone, and the prints end up taped to bedroom walls instead of buried in a camera roll. They’ll fly through the film, so tuck a couple of extra packs in the box.

Searches for the FAO Schwarz Piano Mat “struck a chord,” rising 180% in 2026. Anyone who watched Tom Hanks stomp out a duet on the giant keyboard in “Major” wanted one of these, and the floor-sized version now fits in a playroom. It’s a sneaky music-and-movement toy for preschoolers. It’s also loud, so choose its permanent residence carefully.

Searches for “adjustable roller skates” cruised up 180%. Adjustable skates expand across several sizes, so they can outlast a growth spurt or two. Just remember to add a helmet and pads to the cart.

Some of this may come down to who’s doing the shopping. Millennials make up a big share of today’s parents, and plenty of us spent our childhoods at the roller rink, building wooden train tracks across the living room rug and waiting for Polaroids to develop. (By impatiently wagging them back and forth, of course.) It’s not hard to imagine a few of these searches coming from parents trying to hand down something that felt magic to them. The best part? There’s a good chance they’ll all still be in rotation when next year’s list comes out.
